speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING BUDGETARY DEFICITS
speechtext: I should like to address a question to the Minister of Finance. According to newspaper, radio and television news reports the Prime Minister assured the Canadian Labour Congress yesterday that he saw eye to eye with them on the use of budgetary deficits to assist in the solution of the unemployment problem. Does this announcement indicate a new policy on the part of the government, or does the Minister of Finance have an explanation to make of this apparent conflict with his previous policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING BUDGETARY DEFICITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. member will allow me to reply. I should like to say on the Prime Minister's behalf what he has told me he would have said in answer to this question if he had been in the house. Some press reports have interpreted remarks of the Prime Minister to the Canadian Labour Congress delegation yesterday as if he were taking a view of budgetary deficits different from the view of the Minister of Finance. This is completely without foundation.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING BUDGETARY DEFICITS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING BUDGETARY DEFICITS
speechtext:
The substance of what the Prime Minister said yesterday is what he has said many times before. It is what the Minister of Finance has said many times and

what has been said by many others on behalf of the government and the Liberal party.
We accept the necessity, indeed the desirability, of deficit financing when it is the effective way to stimulate the sound and steady expansion of the economy needed to increase employment. The Prime Minister also believes, as the Minister of Finance believes and the government believes-

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING BUDGETARY DEFICITS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING BUDGETARY DEFICITS
speechtext:
-that it is important not to permit an indefinite continuation of the chronic, very large deficits we have been experiencing. Deficits should be incurred only by deliberate decisions of economic policy; to allow them to continue or to expand indefinitely for other reasons would undermine confidence in the currency and impede steady economic expansion. Therefore one of the objectives of the government should be, and is, to move toward a more balanced budget as the economy gains strength; to see that deficits are reduced with improving economic conditions. That is the government's policy; it is the minister's policy and it is equally the Prime Minister's policy.
The Minister of Finance is making every possible effort to reduce budgetary deficits, among other things by reducing unnecessary expenditures. But he has not hesitated to support expenditures for necessary social and economic purposes, in particular for the reduction of unemployment.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING BUDGETARY DEFICITS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING BUDGETARY DEFICITS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DR. RUSSELL    REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO RESIGNATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wanted to ask the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources a question arising out of the report carried in the press yesterday with regard to Dr. Loris Russell, explaining why he felt he had to get out of the national museum. I wonder whether the minister has any comment to make on this report or any indications as to how he plans to meet the criticisms contained in Dr. Russell's statements, for example by putting them before the house or one of its committees.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: DR. RUSSELL    REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO RESIGNATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read with considerable interest and some dismay the statement attributed to Dr. Loris Russell yesterday. This would seem to culminate a great many years of disturbance within the management of the affairs of the museum. I regret it very much, because Dr. Russell is a distinguished Canadian scientist who indeed in the last several years during which tumult has existed there had contributed enormously to bringing peace and some measure of tranquility to the museum.
I can assure my hon. friend that my one purpose now with regard to the museum is to re-establish over a period of years a degree of tranquility. I am only sorry that Dr. Russell will not be part of it. We have lost not only Dr. Russell but I think six or eight scientists in all, including several holding doctorates. This is an unfortunate state of affairs. I hope it is not a tendency that applies to that particular degree of study. But we are not going to establish a sound museum until internal peace is restored. We propose to make appointments to the museum, the staff of which will be headed by Dr. Glover from the University of Manitoba, and we hope to establish a degree of extended growth and peace in the museum as rapidly as we can.

subtopic: DR. RUSSELL    REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO RESIGNATION
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, which may seem narrow. Dr. Russell in his statement refers to representations that were received which were critical of the course of the museum, particularly from

members of the Canadian historical association. I put a request on the order paper in the form of a notice of motion for the production of papers in relation to these communications. The reply was that there were no communications of this character.
I wonder whether the minister has any explanation for this, because here is a civil servant who knows the correspondence exists, yet the minister has given a reply that there is none available.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: DR. RUSSELL    REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO RESIGNATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member made such a request-I cannot recall it fully now-and we told him there were no such communications, I would say that we told him the truth. However, I noticed the statement of Dr. Russell that pressures had been put upon him to give up his post. I want to say to the hon. member that neither I nor any member of my staff at any time endeavoured to persuade Dr. Russell to leave his post. We were aware that he was dissatisfied in the current post and indeed was hoping, I think, to be made chief of the museum. I think delay in such a decision contributed in part to his discomfiture. However, with regard to the statement that pressures were put upon him to resign, I want to assure my hon. friend that this was not my policy, the policy of the deputy minister or of anyone on the staff.

subtopic: DR. RUSSELL    REPORTED STATEMENT AS TO RESIGNATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, having attended university with Dr. Russell and watched the development of his work in the national museum of Canada over the years, I want to say that in Dr. Russell the Canadian government had one of the finest geologists who ever graduated from a university in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Associate Minister of National Defence in the absence of the Minister of National Defence. speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Cardin (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ANTICIPATED REDUCTION IN ARMED FORCES AND CIVILIAN PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am in a position to inform the right hon. gentleman that a total of 2,293 service and 2,751 civilian personnel will be affected by these reductions. I should point out, however, that in so far as the servicemen are concerned, for the most part they will be transferred to other units to fill vacancies or take the place of others who retire.
As for civilians, approximately 800 are employed on the northwest highway system and at Fort Churchill, and it is expected that there will be little change after the transfer of administrative responsibilities from the Department of National Defence. Of the remainder, positions will be found for some in other government departments in lieu of personnel who would normally be recruited from outside the public service. A few will be retained in the Department of National Defence, where their experience and skills can be used to good advantage.
Every effort will be made to ensure that as many as possible of the employees affected will be taken care of in one way or another, and it is expected that a number will obtain employment in private industry through the agency of the national employment service. I might add that, as my colleague pointed out last week, the discontinuance of or reduction in certain defence establishments will be done on a gradual basis, and every endeavour will be made to minimize any possible hardship or inconvenience for those personnel involved.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I have been in this house-

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: USE OF CHILDREN'S TEETH AS RADIOACTIVE FALL-OUT CHECK
speechtext:
I did not mean any offence to my hon. friend; I meant since my return to the house. I know he has been here when we have been dealing with other legislation, but he has not been in the house during recent question periods. The question asked in my absence while I was at the dominion-provincial conference was taken as notice by my parliamentary secretary, and it is one which requires a fairly elaborate answer.
The information now available to us concerning the University of Toronto project on the measurement of strontium 90 in the primary teeth of Canadian children suggests that a widespread misunderstanding may exist with regard to the purpose of this project. It appears that the study is designed to serve two purposes; (1) to obtain an accurate estimate of the discrimination against strontium 90 as it passes from cows to milk to humans; and (2) to study the uptake of strontium 90 by calcified tissues which have different metabolic properties than bone. From the information available to us there is no reason why these objectives cannot be met by the University of Toronto program. Such studies are of course research studies, and should not be confused with public health monitoring programs.

Inquiries of the Ministry
In my department we are concerned with the public health aspects of nuclear fall-out. The objective in this case is to determine the radiation dose to sensitive tissue such as the bone marrow. The most direct method of assessing the current public health significance of the cumulative effect of fall-out in the past is through a program of measurement of strontium 90 in human bones. My department is engaged in such a study. At the same time we are concerned also with the future significance of fall-out, and for this purpose we have developed a comprehensive nation-wide system of fall-out studies in air, precipitation, soil and food products.
Analyses for strontium 90 in teeth do not provide data which can be used directly for estimating the present or future radiation dose to bone marrow. This is because primary teeth, unlike other parts of the skeleton, are fully formed by the end of the first year of life and there is subsequently little exchange with minerals in the diet. Indirectly, teeth analyses may be used to reflect the levels of strontium 90 in the diet during the period the teeth were formed, that is to say, four to six or more years earlier. If such data are required for public health purposes, a program such as my department's milk monitoring program provides data right up to the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Justice arising out of the sensational disclosures that are again taking place in regard to the Coffin murder trial, namely that the prosecutor has now asked the Quebec bar to investigate his conduct of the prosecution, and a Toronto newspaperman has been implicated in the disappearance of a key piece of defence evidence. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if there is to be a royal commission I am sure the proper place for it is in the province where the trial has taken place, notwithstanding the statements which my hon. friend has made. However, as I said yesterday, my officers are reading the book which has been published by Mr. Hebert to ascertain whether there is any federal aspect to it. I am also reading it myself, and when this reading has been completed if there is any reason to do so, I will make a statement.

subtopic: ALLEGED MISCARRIAGE IN COFFIN CASE
speechtext: I can understand the answer of the Minister of Justice, but I wonder whether an examination has been made with regard to representations which were made following the sentence of death so as to determine whether, during those representations, any of these matters were raised at all.

speechtext: I thank the right hon. gentleman for that question. I think it is going to be very helpful. Yes, Mr. Speaker. I regret not giving the hon. member before now the answer to the question he asked some days ago. I hope he will be tolerant of my absence the last few days. The matter raised by him has to do with the provision made for in transit passengers from a foreign aircraft flying over Canada and landing at Winnipeg for a short time.
This is a matter for decision by the air line concerned, since it is the air line that makes the arrangements for the handling of these passengers on in transit flights. It must determine if it wishes to hold its passengers on the aircraft, have them get off but remain as in transit passengers, that is not cleared by customs and immigration, in which case they may not move around the building, or be cleared by the inspection services so they can circulate freely within the terminal building.
On the flight referred to in the press I gather that the stop was made for 40 minutes only, and that the period of two hours reported in some press stories was not accurate. Accordingly the air line determined that the passengers should be held in transit and not cleared in a way that would permit them to move around the building freely.
Transit facilities at airports normally have limited use. Those in the Winnipeg terminal are comfortable and well furnished. Arrangements have in fact been made to offer additional rooms to the air lines for this purpose when required. If user air lines wish special services provided in these rooms or other adjustments, this is a matter for them to take up with the inspection services or the Department of Transport, according to what their

Pensions Acts
requirements may be. Basically the responsibility rests with the air line concerned for the arrangements it wishes to make for its passengers, and suitable facilities should and can be made available for this purpose.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has suggested that passing such an amendment would not have the effect of causing a delay

Pensions Acts
with respect to these payments. Hon. members would have no reason, I suppose, to understand that these payments are made on the basis of individual agreements signed with each province. Thirty six agreements in all will have to be negotiated and signed in order to make these payments. I asked my department a couple of days ago what would be the latest date by which this legislation could be passed so that we would be sure that the recipients of these assistance payments could receive them before the end of this year. This, unlike old age security, is not a matter where we can mail out cheques in time if we pass a certain date. Agreements cannot be negotiated and signed until we have royal assent. All hon. members of the house know there is about a week to go in which this legislation might be passed in the other place and receive royal assent. After that time the agreements would have to be negotiated. It seems hardly likely it would be possible to have the agreements executed in time for December payments to be made.
There is, however, another point, and it is one which I ask all hon. members to consider. It is this. In this parliament there has been a great deal of talk from all sides of the house about the necessity for agreement, discussion and understanding between the federal government and the provincial governments. This matter was, as the house was frequently advised, on the agenda of the last dominion-provincial conference and was discussed during the whole of the day given over to pension matters. While a number of provincial premiers indicated that their own governments were prepared to match the federal government's share should there be increases under these assistance programs, at the conference, attended as it was by the ministers of health and of welfare of the various provinces, not one premier suggested that there was any merit in a retroactive payment.
The administration of this plan lies not with the federal government but with each of the provincial governments. The hon. member for Perth must know, since he had the responsibility for this department, that there are a number of differences in the way the administration is handled by the various provinces. Their advice to us was that the administrative difficulties were very great in making such payments retroactive. These are assistance programs; most of them are based on satisfying means tests. It is not as simple a matter to administer such programs as it is to date back legislation to make flat rate payments retroactive.

All hon. members have agreed that it is a good thing to consult the provinces in advance. Some hon. members in the house and outside the house have directed certain critical remarks to me, suggesting that I have not consulted others in advance in certain instances. But the course of advance consultation was taken here, because it is not only federal money that is committed, and it is late in the fiscal year. We would be imposing a burden on the provinces, and let us not have any sophistry about this. While it is true that provincial governments may decide whether or not to pay their share, let us have reference, as a matter of practical politics, to the fact that no provincial government could resist the pressure to make the increase available if we had in fact enacted this legislation. Each one of the provinces thus would have to assume a burden for which they did not budget in the spring of this year.
No hon. member in the house can have failed to observe what every provincial representative said in this capital only a few weeks ago; that they were all short of money for the programs which they themselves had already brought in. They were here seeking additional revenue for this purpose. What is involved in this amendment is, I suggest, an invitation to the federal government now, after full consultation, after hearing the opinions of the provincial governments, to act in breach of its word; to deliberately put a gun to the head of each provincial government and say to it "You try and resist the pressure from your own people now. We have really forced you into a deficit position because we have decided upon this. Notwithstanding what you said, we know better".
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is sometimes suggested from the opposite side of the house that we on this side have taken the position that we know better. We have tried to show in our actions with respect to these shared-cost programs our desire to consult with the provinces, who are closer to the people in this respect; and we have, in consultation- as I explained to the house earlier-and after considerable discussion as to how difficult it is to make a retroactive payment of this kind, decided to make it payable at the earliest possible time, which is December 1.
If this legislation is not proceeded with now even that may not be possible, and it may very well be that in at least some provinces the passage of this amendment would result in needy individuals being deprived of this $10 increase. It would depend, of course, upon the final decision of the provincial government concerned. Those who would pass such an amendment must bear the responsibility for that. I ask my hon.

friend, who was minister of this department and I am sure has at heart the best interests of these recipients of such allowances, to consider for himself and his colleagues the position which could result. I ask the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and his colleagues to consider what might happen; and I ask, sir, bearing everything in mind, that the vote be against the amendment and we be allowed to make these payments effective December 1, to keep faith with the provinces and to be sure that we get the money out to these people as quickly as possible.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I mentioned a week or

so ago, I thought that probably many members on the other side of the house were missing me. I realized this when they complained so much that I was away. I am pleased to be here today. I am pleased to present the estimates. I might also suggest that this is a happy time for agriculture.
The main estimates of the Department of Agriculture for the 1963-64 fiscal year total $171,848,900. Of this amount $129,365,900 is to be voted and $42,483,000 is statutory. The statutory items include provision for the payment of carrying costs of temporary wheat reserves and payments in connection with the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act. I should explain to the committee that the present main estimates were drawn up under the previous government and before responsibility for the Canadian wheat board was placed with the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is for this reason that funds required under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act appear in the main estimates of the Department of Agriculture this year.
In addition to the main estimates, two supplementaries have been tabled containing votes for the Department of Agriculture. Supplementary estimates A provide for a total of $372,250, covering various items for which additional funds are required. Supplementary estimates D contain an item for $1 million to provide for the payment of winter storage on western feed grains in eastern position, which I shall refer to later.
In my brief period of office as Minister of Agriculture I have been impressed with the services and the leadership provided by the department to the farming community. It is obvious, of course, that these functions cannot remain static. They must be arranged to meet the changing needs and circumstances of Canadian agriculture, as indeed they have been periodically over the long history of the department.
In the beginning, before the turn of the century, when science was making its first impact on farming, the major preoccupation of the department was in assisting farmers to introduce new cultural and husbandry techniques. This was the period of the inauguration of the experimental farms system and also of the department's veterinary work.
In the earlier part of this century the department's interests expanded gradually into the marketing field, notably in the standardization and grading of a wide range of farm products. The Hon. W. R. Motherwell was particularly responsible for these developments during his period as minister.
The department's entry into the field of rehabilitation and water conservation started

in the 1930's under the leadership of the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner. This was the era which saw the beginning of the prairie farm rehabilitation and maritime marshland rehabilitation administrations. In the 1940's, price supports for farm products became a part of agricultural policy. In the late 1950's, under the then minister, the hon. member for Calgary North, crop insurance was introduced, the Farm Credit Corporation was established to take over and enlarge the previous functions of the farm loan board, and a start was made on a wider rehabilitation program which was subsequently introduced as the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. Thus step by step over many years the activities of the department and its associated interests have been adjusted to meet and serve the needs of Canadian farmers.
In the present circumstances of Canadian agriculture it is becoming clear we are concerned with two broad groupings. On the one hand we have a viable, progressive farming industry made up basically of efficient farms operating on good agricultural lands. Increasingly this is becoming an industry of strong family farm business enterprises. While this side of farming does have occasional difficulties in its various segments, it is essentially in a sound position and is able to benefit from the wide range of government activities in such fields as research, production and marketing policies and credit arrangements.
On the other hand we must recognize that we do have a segment of our agriculture where underemployment is serious, the standard of living low and the size of the operations marginal. This segment, unfortunately, does not benefit greatly from the type of policies which are helpful to the more fortunate section of the farming community. In the main, the less productive segment of our agriculture is located in our poorer land areas, individual operations are small by present standards, and the people concerned endeavour to augment their farm income by other employment. This circumstance is not peculiar to Canada. It is being experienced in many countries and farm policy generally is being shaped to include measures to alleviate the circumstances of people in this lower income segment of agriculture.
The objective of rehabilitation and development programs must be to enable people to stand on their own feet and become a viable part of the economy. The necessity of policies for this purpose is recognized and strongly supported by the government. As an indication of this I might point out that since May 1, 1963, 112 ARDA projects have been approved
Supply-Agriculture
involving expenditure commitments of $4,610,000. This compares with a total of 136 projects approved prior to May 1 with expenditure commitments of $2,119,000, or since May 1 we have almost doubled the dollar expenditure in this area. In addition, in six provinces the government of Canada is financing research projects to secure information on which sound programs of rural development can be initiated in problem areas.
Rural development is a particularly challenging aspect of rehabilitation and the one under which, in co-operation with local interests, the circumstances in less productive farming areas are examined and means sought to improve the employment and income opportunities of the local people. This a complex problem and there is no simple or single approach to it. My department will continue to work closely with other departments of government, with the federal-provincial technical and vocational training programs, with the Department of Industry and particularly the area development agency, and with the Atlantic development board and, of course, the provinces to help assure the kind of co-ordinated approach that is surely required.
It is basic to the rehabilitation program, both P.F.R.A. and ARDA, that we develop as quickly as possible a complete inventory of all our lands now devoted to farming to determine the most appropriate use which can be made of them. We refer to this as the Canadian land inventory. Under this the classification of lands according to their suitability for agriculture is now well under way in co-operation with the provinces. Since I assumed office I have signed agreements with eight provinces to carry on this work at a total cost of $126,000. This is in addition to the resources of my department which are being devoted to it.
The Canadian council of resource ministers has agreed, at our suggestion and with federal financing, to sponsor the extension of this inventory to assess the extent to which present farm lands may be more suitable for forestry, recreation and wildlife. In short, we need this particular inventory as a basis on which to build joint federal-provincial policies and programs.
Soil and water conservation is also extremely important. In addition to substantial action programs under P.F.R.A., M.M.R.A. and ARDA we are working with the provinces on research into longer term water conservation problems. These include irrigation areas in Alberta, ground water supplies in Saskatchewan and water sheds in Ontario.
The present master ARDA agreement with the provinces is in effect until 1965. The agreement was deliberately limited to a three year

Supply-Agriculture
period to enable both levels of government to gain experience on which to develop a sound basis of operations in the years ahead. There will, therefore, have to be extensive consultations over the next year to decide on long term rehabilitation programs. While rehabilitation matters must command our attention, we must be concerned also with strengthening the ability of our farmers to compete with the produce of other countries on export markets and in their home market. This requires continuing attention to efficiency in both production and marketing.
This, if course, is the purpose of research. I am sure that any minister coming to the department would be impressed with the ability and dedication of the scientists who serve agriculture in the department's research activities. We spend considerable money on research. Over 20 per cent of departmental funds are devoted to it. However, the benefits which have flowed to Canadian agriculture have justified those expenditures many times over. In fact, the difficulty is to apportion the available funds to meet the demands for research from different parts of the country and from various segments of the industry.
Since I assumed office, I have visited several of the department's research establishments and have appraised service which they are rendering. I intend to continue this practice as opportunity affords. Some are outstanding. Most are of high calibre. A few need strengthening, both in relation to their programs and in respect of their relations with the farming communities in the areas they serve. The responsible officials are appraising this. I support the requirements for research, believing as I do that research directed to the needs of agriculture is fundamental to our farming industry.
One area where the department's research programs needs to be strengthened is in the province of Quebec. We have decided to establish a research laboratory in association with the faculty of agriculture at Laval University and to develop an enlarged horticultural research station at St. Jean.
I am convinced, too, of the need to strengthen livestock testing programs to ensure that our livestock operations remain fully competitive with those of other countries. This is necessary with beef cattle. It is necessary with hogs. On the matter of livestock, while the department has been able to improve its veterinary staff position to some extent, there is still a basic shortage of veterinarians in Canada, as indeed there is throughout the world. The department employs about 25 per cent of all Canada's veterinarians. To help improve the situation, the government offered to assist to establish a veterinary college in western Canada by
[Mr. Hays.j
contributing 25 per cent of the capital cost to a maximum of $625,000. The western provinces accepted this offer and they have decided the college will be established at the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon. In fact, it is well on its way.
As I said previously, this is necessary with beef cattle. It is necessary with hogs, where we are gradually losing the quality advantage we have enjoyed for our pork in the United States market, as that country improves its hog quality. On my visit overseas this summer, I was impressed with the hog programs in some European countries. I had sent a mission of our technical people to Europe to look into these in depth. As a further step to strengthen livestock testing, we have removed the earlier restrictions on r.o.p. testing for dairy cattle.
On the international trade front, exports of Canadian agricultural products for the first nine months of this year amounted to $861 million, compared to $803 million for the same period last year. All but a small part of the increase is due to expanded wheat sales. For this crop year, exports of Canadian wheat and flour are expected to be in excess of 550 million bushels. The largest quantity exported in any past year was about 400 million bushels. This year we will export 150 million bushels more than in any previous year.
A number of events which could prove significant for the future of agricultural trade have been taking place. As my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, reported earlier this year, a meeting of ministers was held under the general agreement on tariffs and trade in Geneva last May. The ministers then decided that a new round of comprehensive trade negotiations would begin in May 1964, that these negotiations should cover all products, and that they would deal with both tariffs and non-tariff barriers to trade. The non-tariff barriers have assumed particular importance in agricultural trade in recent years.
A trade negotiations committee was established to prepare for the negotiations, and during the past summer they set up a committee on agriculture to consider and submit to the trade negotiations committee recommendations in regard to the rules to govern and the method to be employed in the creation of acceptable conditions of access to world markets for agricultural products in furtherance of a significant development and expansion of world trade in such products. This agriculture committee met recently and made an initial study of the many problems that will be involved in the agricultural negotiations.

For particular products for which special trade arrangements might be more appropriate, such as wheat and coarse grains, meats and possibly dairy products, the GATT ministers decided that special groups should be established as negotiating bodies. The cereals and meat groups have begun their work and a pilot group has been established for dairy products to review the trade problems in dairy products and determine whether a special group would be the most effective way of dealing with these products. The cereals group has agreed to move into actual negotiations early in the new year. These negotiations would be expected to take several months and would aim for a new world grains agreement to cover wheat, flour and the principal coarse grains. These could prove to be important and far reaching negotiations and it is likely that access to important markets as well as production and price policies of both importers and exporters would be brought into the framework of the negotiations.
What progress will, in fact, be made in the over-all agricultural negotiations is not yet quite clear. The members of the European economic community have still not reached agreement among themselves on a number of basic policy decisions about their own agricultural arrangements. The United States has stated on a number of occasions that if progress is not made in the negotiations on agriculture, it will be unable to reduce its industrial tariff. Much will depend on the extent of the participation of these two major trading partners. Canada, of course, will be playing her full part, with the interest of our own relatively efficient agriculture industries very much in our minds.

Reverting now to domestic matters I might say a word about crop insurance. The crop insurance schemes are operated by the provinces. Under the Crop Insurance Act, the federal government supports approved provincial schemes by paying 20 per cent of the premiums and reimbursing the
Supply-Agriculture
provinces for 50 per cent of their administrative expenses. If the claims in any one year exceed reserves plus $200,000, the federal government will lend a province 75 per cent of that.
I am sure we are all hopeful that crop insurance will expand so that farmers may protect themselves against serious crop failures due to circumstances beyond their control. However, an impediment to its expansion, particularly in some of the western provinces, is the concern of the provinces that a serious, widespread crop failure before adequate reserves had been built up may put a severe strain on their financial resources. I can inform the committee that the government is entering into discussions with the provinces with a view to working out an arrangement under which the federal government would be prepared to reinsure a part of the residual risk which now falls completely on the province.
We are also examining whether the present provisions with respect to farm credit are adequate for the present needs of Canadian agriculture. This is a matter of considerable interest to farm organizations and a brief with respect to it has been submitted to me by the federation of agriculture.
The farm credit corporation, at my request, has been studying the matter and examining programs in existence in other countries. I have asked the corporation to undertake a survey of a cross-section of Canadian farmers to determine their views and requirements.
There is a matter which has some association with farm credit which I would like to mention briefly. It is associated also with the net income position of farmers, which is dependant on two considerations. One is the revenue from the sale of produce; the other is farm operating expenses.
Many measures have been taken by governments, at both the federal and provincial level, to help stabilize and improve farm income. Farm operating costs, however, continue to rise and it is becoming increasingly important that farmers, with government guidance and leadership, look for ways to economize in their operating costs. One field which we are exploring is that of farm machinery. In 1961, depreciation on machinery, interest on investment and repairs represented 20 per cent of total farm expenses. A survey of a sample of grain farms in the prairies in 1962 showed that these items contributed about 50 per cent of the expenses there. An additional consideration is the heavy capital cost of farm machinery and equipment, which often is financed at a high interest rate. This capital cost of machinery is, indeed, one of the most serious stumbling blocks to young

has been successful in achieving an increase of about 20 per cent in our cheese production. All present indications are that this increased volume will be handled without serious difficulty. Indeed, I am impressed by the fact that the demand in export markets for top quality mature Canadian cheese exceeds the available supply, and my department is exploring means to direct our dairy assistance program to encourage an increase in the production of this type of cheese.
Mr. Chairman, in all these matters involving agricultural policy it is important that there be close discussion and co-ordination between federal and provincial interests. I met with the provincial ministers of agriculture at their summer conference in Edmonton and we will be meeting again at the federal-provincial agricultural conference here on December 16, 17 and 18. The provincial and federal governments have important roles in the development of policy in the interests of Canadian agriculture. I regard it as important, and I know the view is shared by my provincial colleagues, that there be close liaison between us in the common interest of agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I think it would be an understatement if I said that the house was awaiting the minister's statement with some interest. I think you can readily understand that in view of some remarks which the minister made over the last six or seven months, we were awaiting his statement on these estimates with considerable interest. But now that we have had this statement some of us are wondering what kept it so long, because quite frankly I believe as a Canadian there is a future in farming. However, in view of the minister's statement, I sometimes wonder how that is going to come about, unless there is a very serious realization on the part of the government that fundamental problems now before us need fundamental solutions.
First, I am going to mention a few of the things mentioned by the minister, and then suggest where I think the emphasis should go; because in talking about agriculture we should never lose sight of the fact that a big problem existed, that it was tackled a few years ago, and that we want nothing to interfere with the solution to the problem.
The minister mentioned that there are two broad groups in Canada, the farmer who has
28902-5-367
Supply-Agriculture
adjusted to the conditions of agriculture today and who can be labelled as efficient, and then the marginal farmer. I listened intently as the minister spoke to see if there was any sign that he understood not only the depth of this problem but the fundamental nature of the solutions that must be undertaken.
Not so long ago, on October 14, it was my privilege to move a motion of no confidence in the government on the basis that no action was being taken on a short term solution to meet the problems of eastern farmers. In the over-all picture today we have one basic fact to consider, that with the tremendous and rapid growth of technology in agriculture in the western countries, the industrialized countries where agriculture has almost led the way in technological changes, these countries have a capacity to produce far greater than the ability of their domestic populations to consume.
That fact can be looked upon as a threat to the well being of our farmers, or it can be looked upon as a great asset to be used in the over-all process of developing the income of our country and serving the people of the world in general. When I heard this mention of the two groups I thought we would also hear some indication that there was complete understanding of the necessity of what could be done to take this great ability to produce and harness it for the good of the world, and at the same time have policies in effect that could do something to lift up these farmers in the marginal group.
It was a buckshot treatment of the subject. Some of the matters that I think come close to meeting these two problems were mentioned, but there was no evidence I could find that there was a deep understanding of what the main problem is.
On October 14, when I outlined the extent of this problem, I indicated from the statistics provided by the 1961 census that 43 per cent of the farmers in Canada had a gross income, before deduction of expenses, which could only be considered as verging on slum conditions. The minister spoke after me on that occasion and said that these figures were for losers, and this was all a bunch of junk. I do not know how the people on these marginal farms in Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes feel about his saying their problem is just a bunch of junk, but I did think that after the couple of months elapsed since that speech was made, there would be an indication of some action, and less talk. I say this because away back on October 14 we heard all about what had to be done with respect to machinery costs. The minister said this was going to be studied, but today we are going to study it once again.

Supply-Agriculture
For the minister's information I can tell him we have been studying this problem of machinery since the 'thirties, and there have been innumerable committees set up and innumerable proposals made, but still we wait for the action. A committee was set up during the administration of the previous government, which was trying to get at the basic troubles and was making good progress. However it was cut off with the change of government, and this matter has not come again before the committee on agriculture and colonization.
Therefore I would like to suggest here, with regard to the action that has to be taken, both on behalf of making use of the tremendous capacity to produce of the efficient farmer and finding him markets at remunerative prices and, second, with regard to getting at these marginal farmers' problems, that I listened in vain for some indication of a deep understanding of what these problems implied and the actions that must be taken. Instead, we had this rambling account, covering the whole broad field, without the evidence that there is something deep behind these various suggestions.
Mr. Chairman, I will give you an example of what I mean. The minister said that up until May 1, there had been 122 projects signed under ARDA. Then he said that since May 1, there had been 136 projects signed and, ipso facto, he was doing a better job than the previous government. Well now, I wanted to hear something of his philosophy of ARDA. Is he going to make ARDA purely a question of signing contracts with provincial governments to do certain things, or does he intend to insist in his department that the philosophy of ARDA, agreed on by the provinces and the federal government, shall be maintained?
This philosophy I am talking about is that ARDA will not degenerate into simply doing things like draining a marsh or building a dam, but will go to the guts of the question, which is to raise the farm income in these marginal areas by looking for income opportunities; and if those income opportunities come in any line whatsoever, then they should be made available to the people on that land.
If studies indicate there is over population in some areas, then what is going to be done with that over population? Here is one of the biggest tasks that can be placed before governments all over the world. It applies to many other countries besides our own; but after 50 or 60 years of this problem's developing, finally, in the year 1961, a government took hold of it. There was no intent or intention of trying to solve the problem in one

year, two years, five years or 20 years, but to start the ARDA operation accurately and make it work.
I will give you another example, Mr. Chairman, the philosophy of ARDA is to make every possible use of the land, and if ARDA is narrowed down into just a concept of agreeing with the provinces to build, as I have said, a drainage ditch or a dam, that is not the answer. The answer is to make the best use of that land.
When the minister mentioned the question of the land inventory I hoped he would then mention that this was tied in with the philosophy of ARDA, because this question of land inventory is not new. However he did mention, when he talked about the inventory, that he would look to see if this land could be better used for forestry, recreation or wildlife. This is what I mean by extra opportunities. We must not consider ARDA purely in the traditional sense of agriculture, but rather as a device, as administrative and legislative machinery to make the best use of our land and to increase the income of the people on it.
These various agreements under ARDA will be watched very keenly by those of us in opposition. This is legislation which I think pioneered a concept that was at least equal, if not superior, to legislation in any other country of the world. The provinces support it wholeheartedly. The farm organizations support it wholeheartedly. Where it has been explained to the farmers, in many cases they know it is their only hope. Not only do I plead with the minister to dig into ARDA to try to understand its philosophy and its principles, but I ask that he become the living exponent of it and make sure that it is never narrowed down just to the traditional agriculture, but also exploring of all possible uses to which land can be put.
Still speaking of ARDA, Mr. Chairman, the organization of ARDA is not complete. If we are to carry through to the end the philosophy and principles of ARDA we are going to have to recognize that it must be a completely co-operative venture with the provinces. There can be no more of this business of the federal government deciding every little detail of what the provinces do. This problem is so immense and so close to the people who live in the country that the government closest to the people has the best knowledge of what to do; and when recommendations come up through the ARDA chain-through the group of ministers at the provincial level to the group of ministers at the federal level-the project in question should be looked at to see if it is in conformity with the general understanding of the general ARDA agreement, and there should be no quibbling over dotting

the i's and crossing the t's. It is the provinces' responsibility, and if in the opinion of the federal government these things do not fit into the over-all agreement and are at variance with the principles of ARDA, the provinces have to be told very plainly that the federal government will not support that program any longer. But ARDA will die if you try to control every dollar and cent which is spent. Surely if you make an agreement under the master agreement to cover the principle of a project, the provinces are in the best position to decide whether control should be confined in the first place to the local level. All that we should be concerned with is whether it follows the principles of ARDA, and we should make sure that the provinces do not abuse it in any way, go beyond the principles of ARDA or narrow down its concepts. So I say that there is need for a comprehensive look at the requirements of the country, and that is the job of ARDA at the federal level. Let the details of the administration and supervision of these projects rest largely with the provinces. Certainly we can maintain control of our dollars invested in them by a general perusal of those programs; but if we kill off each program by watching every nickel spent and by taking a year to decide whether or not a project should be approved, it is the quickest way to stop any progress under ARDA.
Still following along the line of the concept of redevelopment, the minister mentioned water conservation. He also mentioned irrigation in Alberta and groundwater table surveys in Saskatchewan; and I think he mentioned one more. These are good in themselves, and I have worked hard and long to get that groundwater survey started. But I waited today for one of the most important statements that the minister could have made. Speaking now of western Canada, surely he must be aware that for many years the great need of western Canada has been for a physical and economic survey of the Sas-katchewan-Nelson river system. Surely he must be aware that the western Canada reclamation association and the South Saskatchewan river development association have both pleaded with governments to bring forward some form of joint study. Surely he must be aware that the federal government proposed to the three provincial governments concerned that we be all prepared to share the financing.
I know that this matter is one of constant interest, but I want the minister to know what is our feeling on this side of the house about this study. This is not just a study of the amount of water that flows down the river. We can ascertain that just by looking at the records of the northern affairs water resources branch. What we want to know is 28902-5-3674

what are all the forms of water which we can get the use of over the next 30 to 40 years in the west. This has to be a co-operative study because the economic study of the area will lead to solutions which must be reached co-operatively. What I am frightened of is that some single department-I am referring to northern affairs and national resources-will say: "We want to do this study because we have a water resources branch".
If that happens, Mr. Chairman, the first thing the government will run into is the opposition of one or two of the provinces. The machinery for this study is ready now. We have the prairie provinces water board with three members from the provinces on it and two members from the federal government. This board should be authorized to carry out the study. The study should be speeded up, because we have wasted the last two or three years trying to get agreement with one of the provinces, and now that province shows signs of giving its agreement. This study should be both physical and economic. I am looking at all the possibilities of that river basin. I suggest that this prairie provinces water board realize that the P.F.R.A. organization has certain opinions; they realize that the P.F.R.A. has certain machinery to carry out the big aspects of the study. They know what the Saskatchewan research council is doing in this matter. With all this information available I ask them not to duplicate what is being done but to correlate it and fill in the gaps. I suggest strongly that this is something which would indicate that there is a comprehensive approach to redeveloping many of these areas of Canada; and on this particular aspect I am speaking about the prairies.
I am going to skip some of the subjects, Mr. Chairman, because I realize that I have not time to cover them all, and I am turning now to the question of the eastern farmer. Generally speaking, if one measures the health of agriculture by looking at the realized net income per farm over the past 10 or 12 years, this is the best knowledge that we have of finding out where the trouble lies. It is obviously not the final way but it is the best way that we know. I put on the record of the house two months ago some of the income statistics per farm by province and regions so as to indicate in a general sort of way how the income in the prairie provinces in the last five years has risen and is beginning to look fairly good. It is coming up. In Ontario it is just fair because the income of the good farms is balanced off by the low level of income from the marginal farms. In Quebec it can only be described as poor. There is an increase but it is a poor

Supply-Agriculture
level of increase. In the maritimes it can only be described in one short word, "bad". If we are going to look at the health of agriculture-and the income figure tells us where its health is bad-surely there should be a concentration of interest on the problem of the marginal farmer who has not been able to adjust, at the same time not letting down on our program to help the efficient farmer.
What evidence did we have in the minister's statement that there was a real and serious effort to get at this program? Almost none. What the minister said was that we are voting $1 million in these estimates and the supplementary estimates to pay for storage for grain stored in eastern positions for domestic use. He thought that this would answer all the eastern farm problems; that this would bring down, and has brought down, a sufficient supply to meet the needs. I am not going to repeat what has been happening in the standing committee, Mr. Chairman. I am going to put it in this way. There is a long range problem here. We have set up the machinery, both legislative and administrative, under ARDA to look after the long range program of adjustment. But we have to remember that there are short-range measures we can take, I should like to suggest five or six in number.
One of these is to get at the biggest single cost of the eastern farmer, the cost of feed grain. The minister suggests that by spending $1 million for storage in terminal elevators in Montreal, Quebec, Three Rivers, Halifax and other places this whole problem will be solved. I simply say, as I said on October 14, that this will not solve the problem. A farmer who is feeding stock wants to know what the price will be for the six months he is feeding. He wants to have stability of price. I do not know why the government shies away from this. This whole matter has been discussed in the committee, and we are working there. As you may know, Mr. Chairman, between 15 and 18 Progressive Conservative members, not only from the east but from the west, are there attending the committee every day, attempting to find some solution to this problem. Drawing evidence from witnesses is, sometimes, like pulling deeply rooted teeth, but slowly and inexorably we are reaching the point where we can make suggestions. Even if this government has no suggestions to make, the rank and file of that committee do have suggestions which will meet the needs of eastern agriculture.
There is no secrecy about it. We had a bill ready a year ago. The whole of this year has been wasted. Nothing has been done about the long range task of stabilizing the price of feed to eastern producers, who need to know what the price will be over the whole

of the six months period. The eastern farmer is not complaining about the price the western farmer is getting. He is complaining because when he starts to feed he cannot be sure the price will remain stable. In the past the price has gone up during the feeding operation, and as a result eastern farmers have lost their investment. We have been waiting to see whether an announcement would be made on the occasion of these estimates to show that the government had produced a policy to meet the situation. But we are disappointed.
The minister went further and told us there should be some body set up to provide liaison between all the agencies of government and private business concerned with the supply of feed grain. I do not wish to go into detail about the work of the committee but I think the questions which were put to the witnesses and the answers which members of the committee received indicated that this suggestion cannot possibly meet the needs of the eastern feeders. I know this proposal was put forward by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, but the representatives of that body did not look like very happy witnesses after they had been questioned by the members of the committee. Once again, the government is shying away from the main problem.
A government which is not prepared to move to help eastern agriculture in the face of the figures on record should not be sitting on the government side of this house. I speak harshly on this question because I feel deeply about it. The minister must be aware that a study was made last January of conditions in the five eastern provinces. I asked the provincial governments to pick areas in Ontario, Quebec and the three maritime provinces where income was below the average level. We sent in competent people to interview the farmers in these areas in depth. This study is now available to the hon. gentleman. I do not intend to ask for its reproduction, though I sometimes wish that a summary of it might be published. I honestly believe that if the people of Canada were made aware of the situation in 22 areas of eastern Canada, as disclosed in that study, the shame of it would force any government into taking action.
There are many things to be done. I suggested that we have five or six in mind. The first is to stabilize the price of feed grain, and this is going to be done, if the opposition has any say.
To return briefly to the situation of the efficient farmer. The efficient farmer has a tremendous capacity to produce. We have demonstrated that if we go out and search for markets, as we have done in the case of markets for grain, these markets can be

found. Today we face a prospect that by the end of 1965 the western farmer producing bread grain can increase his production by 15 or 20 per cent, using all the techniques available to him. I am not the least pessimistic about that. What a contrast with what was said in the Gordon commission report, in 1956, to the effect that we could look forward only to exporting 250 million bushels of wheat a year until 1980. Today, in 1963-64, not only are we going to hit an export figure of 550 million bushels, as has been suggested by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but our exports are likely to exceed 600 million bushels and be closer to 625 million bushels. Russia has now come into the market as a regular buyer requiring definite quantities of wheat. The countries behind the iron curtain are saying they want to trade with us on a permanent basis. China wants to trade with us on a permanent basis. In these circumstances we must look forward to providing for export at least 400 million bushels a year. All this shows what can be done. I wish to turn, now, to eastern agriculture.
Who is carrying the mail for the dairy industry today? All we have heard today is that 15 million pounds of surplus butter have been got rid of. Is this the answer? The minister said the cheese market has been expanded. That is good, but I am thinking about a world which needs proteins and which is willing to pay for them if the stuff is available for sale. I know there are limitations. We have allies in New Zealand and Denmark, friendly democratic countries, and we would not think of putting our products on the world market at a dump figure. If the world price for butter is 32 cents. I am sure no Canadian government would sell it for less. If they did, and if, as a consequence, the world price fell to 27 cents or 28 cents, a serious charge could be laid against the minister that in exporting our surplus he had lowered the world price to the great detriment of our friends in Denmark and New Zealand.
I listened carefully to what the minister said about the desirability of an international agreement covering flour and coarse grains. Discussions in this direction should include dairy products, because this is the field in which agreement is most needed. We are, fortunately, in a sellers' market for grain and we can talk good terms. Today, the need is in the dairy industry. The answer to the difficulties of that industry will not be found in making a modest change in the price of cheese or in the price of skimmed milk powder, though all this helps. I have before me a speech made by Mr. Hannam-the last speech of a man who had given over 20 years of service to the farmers of this country. He says that short term solutions are not enough; there
Supply-Agriculture
must be long term solutions. This particular speech was delivered in January, 1963. Then he went on to deal with the dairy industry. He said the government was working with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to reach a national dairy policy. Well, I have not heard anything about this idea in the last eight months, although it was conceived more than a year ago. I have not heard of the birth of any policy. Has there been an accident in the meantime? Has there been a stillbirth? I do not know. But I do know this: The dairy farmers of Canada, particularly of Ontario and Quebec, expect some action to be taken by this government, not just a few words about what is happening to the price of butter, and so on. There is to be discussion with the provinces, not only next summer, at the summer conference, but in the conference to be held next week.
I would hope that the minister would concentrate on the problem of a national dairy policy. We had a conference on February 22 last. There was an election on April 8 and the government changed on April 22. I have waited all this time for some sign that the little idea we started with over a year ago resulting in the conference on February 22 last is going to flower into something tangible, because in addition to looking at the short term situation you have to look at the long term.
My time is nearly up. I could discuss crop insurance, net income and a few other things, but I think I have made my point clear.

I will still shorten my remarks because I do not want to trespass on the committee. The minister likes to say that he is a pretty knowledgeable person with regard to agriculture. When any person points out the terrible conditions that exist in some segments of agriculture, he likes to say that this is junk. But he has come out today with this bits and pieces type of announcement that indicates to me he has no concept whatsoever of a broad, comprehensive policy to get at the fundamental needs of agriculture. Fortunately, even though he does not recognize it, he is operating today on the momentum of the seven point program announced in the house on August 20, 1958, and put into legislative form and administrative practice in the years that followed, which today is moving agriculture to higher and higher plateaus. As long as he does not understand it, fine; but I hope that with all the juggling he is doing he will not rock the boat.

speechtext: We can consider that when the Speaker is in the chair. At the moment we are still in supply. The hon. member for Timiskaming.

Mr. Chairman, we have waited for some time, as I am sure agriculture has waited, for a statement from the minister which I presumed would follow along the lines of the speech he made, indicating that there were at least four major problems facing agriculture today. We are surprised and I am sure all those connected with agriculture will be surprised at the statement made by the minister today, a statement prepared by civil servants revealing some of the problems of agriculture. Having read some of the minister's own speeches I am sure the one today is not in the same category.
Some things have been said this afternoon by the former minister of agriculture which I think warrant a reply by the minister, and I will be very interested in that reply because since I have been in the house there has always been a tendency to say to the government of the day: You are just carrying on something we started; you are simply amending it and making it a little better. In this case I would think it would be very difficult

to carry that very far because there does not seem to be much change in the situation at all.
In my opinion agriculture is in a very bad condition in much of Canada. It is quite true that the government through various agencies has been very successful in the marketing of one of our major products, wheat. It is quite true that we were very fortunate, and this really has nothing to do with government but is related to climatic conditions and the ability of the farmers to grow wheat, in that we were able to harvest a bumper crop of wheat in western Canada and have been able to sell a large portion of it through various agencies. We have now reached a stage, Mr. Chairman, where we must ask ourselves, if we remain as a prime exporter of wheat, whether or not we are holding sufficient grain in storage to take care of any calamity that may occur, such as has happened to other exporting nations. If such an event occurred, would we be in a position to take care of our needs for a sustained period of several years? I would think with the maintenance of the stock this year, we probably will be in no worse position in this regard than we were in former years.
However, I believe that before long a study has to be initiated of the potential of Canadian agriculture and our role as an exporting nation, in order that we can be sure of maintaining sufficient stock to take care of the fluctuations that are inherent in an agricultural economy. As we all know, the crop depends on the weather and we should maintain good stocks in storage as a protection for the years when crops may not be up to standard. The situation in which Russia finds itself today could easily be repeated in Canada because, to some extent, we are subjected to the same kind of climatic conditions. Over the years, Russia has built up production, and this year they find themselves faced with their terrific shortage because they did not maintain sufficient stock in storage.
The Minister of Agriculture has several thoughts of his own in that October 14 speech. One of these related to the problem of farm machinery. I am not sympathetic to a government-and I am not referring just to this government but to the previous government as well-which has committees available on which there are agricultural people with some knowledge of this subject and who are willing to spend their time discussing these particular subjects, but who are not used by the government. I blame the previous government for not reconstituting the farm machinery committee after it had done so much work in this particular field. In October the Minister of Agriculture said he felt the high cost of farm
Supply-Agriculture
machinery was one of the major problems and therefore, I expected he would do something about it. I believe the statement he made was considered by other agencies. I refer particularly to the Searle Grain Company which, in one of their publications, mentioned this problem in an article entitled, "Farm Machinery Costs Bearing Upon the Small Farmer." I quote in part from this article:
It would be interesting to know exactly what the Minister of Agriculture had in mind the other day when, in discussing some of the major problems faced by western farmers, he suggested that "if we are going to have the family farm we must have some sort of rental deal whereby the fanner will be able to rent the machinery he needs when he has good crops."
We have always been quite interested in this subject. From time to time various Department of Agriculture officials and economists have warned that operational efficiency could be seriously affected through over-capitalization in farm machinery. At the same time they have cautioned against purchasing sizes and types of farm machinery that were uneconomic to the farm operator. Others have gone so far as to say one of the main reasons for the difficulty facing many of the small farm operators in western Canada can be traced to an over-investment in high priced farm machinery-that is the purchase of combines, swathers or other high priced units by operators whose size of farm or scale of operations could not possibly justify such an outlay or provide an opportunity for the full utilization of the equipment purchased.
There is no indication that this matter is going to be discussed in the statement the minister made today. He certainly did not refer to any activity that would indicate the subject was going to be discussed, yet it is one of the major issues faced by the government.
There are other things which the minister mentioned, such as the credit we need to make farm units economical. The Farm Credit Corporation was good, but not good enough, said the minister. Our third big problem is crop disaster-that is, when many farmers had their crops hailed out, dried out, blown out or frozen out. There are farmers who need help, and the sooner we do it the better. The minister asked: "How can we do it when we waste so much time in this house? I have never seen such a waste of time; it is just fantastic." I do not think the minister needs to worry about that. He is the least well known member of this house. He is almost unknown in his own department. I have talked to officials who have never met the minister. He need not worry about the time wasted here. I do not believe this is good enough for agriculture. I think we need to do something about it, and the Canadian public are demanding that we do something about it.
I should like to adjourn this debate and return to this subject at seven o'clock.

speechtext:
It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7 p.m.
1. Departmental administration including the national co-ordinating committee on agricultural services, $1,057,600.

Mr. Chairman, before the recess I was commenting on the fact that the minister in a speech in October had indicated that one of the things needed in this area was assistance to the dairy industry. I think this is a field to which the minister should give his full attention. We thought at one time that the second minister of agriculture would probably work in this field, and we have been surprised that so little has been accomplished in this respect. In the field of eastern agriculture, particularly in the dairy industry, there is room for expansion and government assistance, because the dairy industry has not by any means reached a capacity position and if assistance is given it is quite likely there will be an expansion in almost every part of that industry.

Ontario has given consideration to some of the problems. A speech made recently by the minister of agriculture of Ontario indicated their desire to explore the methods of marketing agricultural products, and lamented the fact that some difficulty had been experienced in maintaining the agreements negotiated between producer and distributor in the dairy industry. There has been, and is, government interest in the field of establishing grades in the dairy industry, particularly in the matter of cream, and establishing a price based on quality of the product rather than just on the quantity. We are all aware that some fields, such as the premium export of cheese, the field of unpasteurized cheese for export, can be greatly increased. This is a field for which there is a large market in Europe and it is a market we have not been able to satisfy for some time.
Perhaps some hon. members are not aware of the fact that much of the cheddar cheese produced in Ontario and eastern Canada today is generally of the quick pasteurized type which is difficult to sell in Britain, in particular, because of the difficulty in maintaining a grade. However, cheese that is naturally cured has a ready market and is a field which I think many cheese producers should be encouraged to enter. Additional assistance should be provided which will allow for the storage facilities necessary in competition between the two types of cheese. In producing milk the dairy industry has also run into many problems to which I was very surprised to learn the federal Department of Agriculture had given little consideration.
The problem of surpluses has bugged the dairy industry, particularly the fluid milk industry, over the years; but now the industry has found a new way of making use of milk surpluses, converting them into sterile milk which is manufactured under the trade name of multimilk. This is a development which is quite prevalent in northern Ontario, and I should at once point out that there is nothing wrong with multimilk. Through a process of vacuuming, manufacturers are now able to sterilize products, removing the bacteria from them so that, for example, when meat is packaged it can sit on a store shelf without refrigeration for several weeks without any deterioration in its quality.
Multimilk is a vacuum treated, water removed product which the housewife can leave on a kitchen table or shelf for quite a period of time. She has only to add water to the product, in the ratio of two quarts to one, to turn it into liquid milk. However, the complaint of the dairy industry, particularly the fluid milk industry, is that this milk which is coming on to the market as a fluid milk is not classified by the department as

a fluid milk but as a processed product; yet it is in competition with fluid milk.
This is further complicated by the fact that the milk which goes into its manufacture is bought at surplus prices. Normally fluid milk in Ontario is marketed at over $5 a cwt. while surplus milk fetches only $2.85 a cwt. Yet when the surplus milk is processed it has a premium price over fluid milk, but the farmers only get the surplus milk price for it.
There is another side to this problem. One has only to walk into a grocery store and look at the dairy counter to find pounds and pounds of what appears to be butter, but on examination it will be seen to be margarine. This product is now coloured and has the appearance of prints of butter. However the farmer gets very little protection against this unfair type of competition. A government that is interested in helping the farmers will give consideration to these matters.
The minister did bring out some good points, and in this connection I would like to point out that many Liberal candidates in the last election talked about farm credit and the extension of credit to help make good, economic, farm units. There is nothing more important to the farmer than the ability to establish good credit, and to get the money necessary to make his farm an economic unit. However the Liberal candidates failed to point out to the farmers that credit in itself is not necessarily a good thing.
Because I have a job and can go down to a finance company and borrow $2,000 or $3,000 does not necessarily mean it is a good thing for me to borrow it, unless I have some purpose for its use, some project that will bring me a return, that will enable me to pay off the loan and still be able to maintain my family or my operating unit on an economical basis. In fact, the department itself in its publications stresses this fact, and in the Farm Credit Corporation publication, "Credit for Profit" it says:
"Credit for profit" is a short way of saying that the borrowed dollars should be used to provide an increased income which will pay all operating and maintenance costs, give the farmer and his family a good living, and provide for the orderly repayment of the required credit.
This is often forgotten. In my constituency the Liberal candidate went around telling the farmers, "You have not been able to get credit under the Conservative government. We will give you your loans; just make the application." If this had happened it would have put half the farmers in Timiskaming out of business. A farm credit loan, based on a mortgage on the land, is only an acceptable credit if the farmer can prove to the person making the loan that there is a chance
Supply-Agriculture
to pay it back, and at the same time maintain his farm as an economic unit.
This matter of credit has been considered by the house several times in recent years, and the results have been fairly satisfactory. There is no question but that when we discuss this there will be complaints and some talk about the fact that all the lawyers handling the mortgages change as soon as the government changes. Patronage applies in the legal section as well as in others, but this is not my point. I believe that agriculture is an industry that is as valuable to Canada today as it has ever been. It is an industry that needs assistance because it is highly automated. The farmer must be given assistance to help him package and deliver his products to the consumer, whether the product be grain, free of glass, or any other commodity.
The farmers of the nation deserve better for their contribution to it. We have heard there is going to be a cabinet shuffle. Certainly we need it in this portfolio, because I do not think the minister is interested in his department. I do not think he is interested in the things that go on in the department. In all honesty he should say whether he is going to be in Ottawa and will do something in the department, or not. There are Liberal members of the agriculture committee who are trying to do something on behalf of farmers, and I am sure the farm organizations will want some change made in the department.
