I would go further, Mr. Chairman, and say that the assistant minister, who is to be designated as the eastern representative of agriculture, has done even less than the minister. Nobody has been filling this portfolio, and anyone who wanted it could step into it.
For several weeks on the agriculture committee I have sat with many young Liberals who are interested in agriculture. It is not for us to question whether the voters were right in deciding they would only send one Liberal from the prairies to parliament, but there are young progressive farm representatives in the Liberal party who have made a great contribution to the agriculture committee. I see two of them now sitting behind the minister, both the chairman and vice chairman of the agriculture committee, and I think they have an honest desire to see that something is done in agriculture.
I strongly recommend that the Prime Minister give consideration to some of these young people. If they did not want to, they would not have sat on the agriculture committee, and I would point out that that committee had a great time getting the minister to attend it for one afternoon.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest he resign. Agriculture deserves a better deal than it is getting. The minister on numerous occasions has said

Supply-Agriculture
that this place is a waste of time, that he has never seen such a fantastic waste of time. If he thinks this, then he has an obligation to the Prime Minister and his other colleagues in the cabinet to do something about it.
Yesterday I sat for an hour and a half listening to the Canadian Labour Congress present its brief to the government. It was generally agreed by everybody there that they were quite happy with the reception they received from the government. I kept thinking of the situation that prevailed a year or two ago, when the former prime minister exercised some influence in this field, and that was not the feeling then. I think the situation has changed from the position where labour was not the white-haired boy to the position where it is now that. On the other hand farmers are not any longer sure they are getting a hearing from the government and have lost faith in the Minister of Agriculture's ability to help them. They deserve better than this and I think the minister, who has had some success in other fields, would be fair to his colleagues to take this into consideration.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the members of this group we welcome this occasion, which is the first time the minister has made a major speech to outline a broad, general review of some of the agricultural policies his government has undertaken since it took office. In the few minutes available to me this evening I want to make a general statement of policy on behalf of my party and to indicate to the minister and the government some of the things we support and some of the things to which, at least up to this point, we think they have not paid sufficient attention.
Before I go to that I should like the minister and all hon. members of this committee to know that we in this group consider agriculture still to be the most important industry in Canada. For that matter it is still the most important industry in the world. Whether the meaning can be given to the remark of the minister during some of the debates which have taken place in this house about its being a waste of time, I do not know. If that is what he means, we violently disagree with him. I should like him to know that the success or failure of an organization as large and of such magnitude as that of the European economic community is in jeopardy today because not enough time has been spent over agreement on agricultural policies. I heard on the radio news broadcast yesterday that the French delegate to negotiations now under way in Brussels walked out of the discussions and went back to his government for further instructions. The reason is because President 
de Gaulle of France is demanding that agricultural policy within this market be determined now; he is not willing to wait any longer. In fact, he has indicated that unless this agricultural policy is determined very soon he may even withdraw France from the whole agreement within the European economic community.
I should like also to point out to the minister and the government that there is an article in the Christian Science Monitor indicating that the whole "Kennedy round" of negotiations respecting GATT and the E.E.C. is going to fail unless a satisfactory solution is found to our agricultural policies. In other words, agriculture to Europe, particularly to France and even to the United States, is so important that all their other agreements respecting trade will break down unless they can come to some mutually satisfactory arrangement over agriculture. I just want to make it abundantly clear that even the most highly industrialized nations of the world, such as the United States, France, and so on, regard agricultural policy as paramount, with the exception perhaps of defence. The previous prime minister had this to say, and I am not sure whether he was in the house at the time because my source does not indicate that. He said:
Trade has become a major weapon in the communist offensive. They do not care about profits. Their profits will be measured by the numbers of souls who trade their survival as free men for the temporary material advantage of the present.
So I suggest that even the past prime minister has indicated that agriculture and trade policies are of major importance.
On one or two occasions the Minister of Agriculture has referred to our surplus foodstuffs as being something of a problem. I think it would be well for him to take the attitude that a surplus of food is not a curse btu is in fact a blessing. It is far better that we have surpluses than shortages. We need only look to the countries behind the iron curtain, for example, who have been unable to develop production techniques that can fill the food requirements of their own people. I think the minister will agree that their problems are far greater than ours with our surplus food production.
I also suggest to the government that Canada can play an important role internationally as a major food supplier. We have said this on a number of occasions, and I suppose some hon. members are getting a little tired of hearing us say that Canada's ability to produce food could be a major item in our external policy, our foreign aid policy and our peacekeeping policy.
There is one other aspect of trade and agriculture which I think is worthy of

mention. I have before me some newspaper articles. I will not read them all, but I have one from Washington which indicates the amount of dollars Canada is spending on agricultural products from the United States. A figure amounting to something like $517 million annually is spent in the United States on agricultural products which are imported into Canada. Yet from time to time we have a serious balance of payments problem with the United States. In fact, the problem is chronic; it occurs each year. We imported $80 million worth of corn from the United States last year. At the same time we produced in Canada, not necessarily at points where it was most needed, grain, feed grains particularly, which could be substituted for a lot of these items we are getting from the United States.
There is one other matter we should take note of during discussion of agricultural estimates-although the Canadian wheat board, which deals with this matter, has been transferred to the department under the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who answers to parliament for their activities-and that is the matter of selling large quantities of grain on the international market, particularly to Russia and China. I think the sales over the last few months have proven for all time that the ex-minister of agriculture, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, has not any exclusive claim to being a wheat salesman. When conditions are right and there is the demand, the Canadian wheat board can and does sell large quantities of wheat whether or not the hon. member for Qu'Appelle happens to be occupying the seat of the minister of agriculture. It should be clearly pointed out too that the claim of the Conservative party that they initiated this kind of program falls by the wayside. If hon. members would take a quick glance at history they would see that one of the first deals made on a credit basis was the deal with Poland when wheat was sold under a long term credit agreement. These sales to Russia, and the additional sales to China since that government was turned out of office, simply prove to me-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
No. The hon. member will have ample opportunity to make his own contribution. My time is limited to 30 minutes.
I should like to hear about the position of the hon. member's own party with regard to these sales to communist countries.

There is one thing which can be said as far as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and his party are concerned.
Supp ly-Agricu Iture
Let us hear about your party.

It is abundantly clear that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is a champion of publicity and public relations. For taking credit to himself for whatever was done, he is unexcelled. Never before in our history has any minister spent so much out of public funds in order to advertise a political party. I think this is something of which the Canadian people should be aware. For example, we know now, though we did not know it then, that the former minister of agriculture got himself flown over to Hong Kong at public expense to make an announcement that a deal had been made, three days after the contract had been signed. I am sure this was good for the Conservative party, and the very fact that it was to the benefit of that party seems to impose an obligation to pay for that flight. But this trip was paid for out of public funds. Almost every day, for months on end, we could look into our mail boxes and see some press release or pamphlet or other publication from the Department of Agriculture. So I give the hon. member full credit for all this publicity. Whether it was good for Canada or not, is questionable. Certainly, it was good for the Conservative party.
I agree with the remarks the minister made concerning farm credit. I think all parties in this house, possibly all members of this committee who have interested themselves in agriculture, will agree that the supply of credit to maintain the family farm, for which we all have respect, is one of the most vexing problems we face in this country today. I agree, also, that the cost of farm machinery, its maintenance, depreciation and so on, constitutes one of the major difficulties to which we must give attention. I believe the minister said that in 1962 the cost of machinery in Canada generally accounted for about 20 per cent of the total operating costs. I believe he went on to say that in one area of western Canada they amounted to 50 per cent of all operating costs. I know from personal experience that this is so. The price of farm machinery has increased tremendously. I cannot blame the manufacturers for putting up their prices. I know that the farmers-and I am one of them-keep demanding bigger and more spectacular equipment. I happen to know that my father, farming in 1940, was able, for example, to cultivate his land with one tractor of 45/50 horsepower. Now it seems we need three of them to work the same 2,500 acres. Most of the time, these machines are doing nothing. In former days, it seemed we had men to run this one 45 horsepower tractor 24 hours a day.

Supply-Agriculture
I think there is a great deal to be said in favour of the establishment of machinery pools, or co-operatives, or similar arrangements so that farm machinery could be used for many more hours than it is being used today. I say this from personal experience, because my brothers and I are able to make use of the same equipment on each of our farms. In other words, we do not each buy the same item. Sometimes this equipment is only in use for three or four weeks of the entire year. Possibly it is in use for only two weeks. This sharing arrangement has certainly reduced our costs substantially, since depreciation takes effect only on one unit instead of on three. There is a great deal which could be done in this direction.
I should like to refer, now, to this report put out by the Searle Grain Company Limited, to which the hon. member for Timis-kaming referred. This publication discusses the advisability of forming machinery pools in order to cut down operating costs. I notice the hon. member did not quote from the end of the article where it says:
Whether or not it might be possible for groups of farmers in western Canada to form a local association in this way we cannot say.
Then, a little further on, the report says:
We agree that if something were to develop along the lines suggested by the minister, it might be very desirable.
The article goes on to say that some leadership in this field would have to be given either by the federal or the provincial departments of agriculture. I really fail to see what the departments of agriculture, either provincial or federal, can do except to urge farmers to take part in such arrangements. If such a scheme is to be effective, the farmers themselves must initiate it in cooperation with their neighbours. I can visualize serious problems arising if two or three farmers owned one combine capable of harvesting the crops of two or three farms. Weather conditions being as uncertain as they are, there would likely be a dispute as to who was to get it first, and if one farmer got in his crop while another was hailed out, the government would be in a precarious position in deciding what was to be done about the lost harvest supposing it was connected, as a sponsor, for example, with the sharing agreement. For this reason I think any such scheme should be worked out among the farmers themselves.
I was pleased to see that in the last wheat deal with the Soviet union provision was made for a certain portion of that wheat to be supplied in the form of flour. This is the first time in several years that the flour milling industry of this country has had a break. We heard the hon. member for
Qu'Appelle, who was minister of agriculture at that time, say that provision had been made for at least some portion of the wheat sold to China to be delivered in the form of flour, or the finished product. But to my knowledge there was not one single bushel of those 112 million bushels delivered in the form of flour. I should like to point out that between 1956 and 1962 there has been a steady decline in the production of the flour mills in Canada. In 1956, the amount of flour produced here was 4,071,437 cwt. By 1962 this amount had dropped to 2,202,828 cwt. In fact, it has been cut almost in half despite the fact that in 1962 there was more flour traded on international markets than at any time in history. Canada has not lost only in absolute terms; we have lost even more in terms of our relative share of the world market. The Department of Trade and Commerce, the Canadian wheat board or the Department of Agriculture, whichever was responsible, should be congratulated for making sure, in the course of these negotiations, that the deal with Russia provided for the inclusion of a reasonable amount of flour. As a matter of fact, the total unused capacity of the flour milling industry of Canada will be entirely taken up by the 29.1 million bushels of flour content provided for in the agreement. So we could not have sold them any more flour even if they had wanted more. I want to acknowledge this and to thank whoever is responsible, because this is the first break that the flour milling industry has had and they are now assured of being able to run at full capacity until July 31 of next year. Sometimes there is a tendency toward a chain reaction in regard to these things. I have been in touch with some of the managers of the mills, whom I know since the Russian deal, and I have learned that some of their regular customers have been sending in more orders than they were a year ago. This is all well and good for the next ten months. We acknowledge it is a good thing but we are a little apprehensive about what is going to happen after that.
We think it is the responsibility of the government to give priority to the setting up of deals for flour and so on in the international field, so that we will have regular customers on a continuing basis. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle suggested that the dealings with China and the countries behind the bamboo and iron curtains are probably going to be on a permanent basis. I am really not prepared to accept at the moment that they will be buying flour or wheat from us when their own production meets their demands, as it apparently did prior to 1960.

I want to turn now for a moment to ARDA. The act was brought in several years ago and a lot of publicity was given to it. We were told by the Progressive Conservative members, who were running round the country at that time, that the act was all-embracing, that it was very broad and that it was going to solve all the problems of agriculture. It was broad, all right, but it was so vague in its terms that nobody knew anything about what was intended-that is specifically what projects would be acceptable. As a matter of fact, I do not believe that the provincial and local ARDA committees yet have a clear concept of what specific projects the federal government has in mind.
It is because the provincial government of Alberta will not co-operate.

We have all these people, like the former minister of agriculture, pointing out all the problems. He has analysed the problems. But then he winds up by saying the government should do something about them. If there is anything that leaves me cold it is a long discourse about problems, and then no suggestions as to what should or can be done about them. This is exactly what took place before the ARDA bill was introduced. The Conservative members of that day pointed out all the things that were wrong with agriculture and all the problems of the farmers of eastern and western Canada. Then the government of that day introduced a bill that said, in effect: "We are in favour of doing everything that is good for the farmers," -and that is about all.
I do not believe we need any further studies on some of these matters. It has even been suggested that we need to have another study of the South Saskatchewan river basin. I happen to know there is a royal commission report in the hands of the government now and I have a couple of copies in my office. I refer to the Hogg commission which studied this matter.
In what year?

In my view what we need for the farmers of this country is some action and not more studies. As far as specific projects are concerned, one hon. member mumbled something which I understood to be: What is your solution; what is your suggestion? I have many suggestions. There is the matter of community pastures, a project that should get under way right now. There is the matter of upper level storage for the drainage basins. I do not know whether the hon. member for Macleod is here tonight, but he has talked about all these things year in and year out. In 1957 they were going to do them then.
Supp ly-A griculture
In 1962 they were going to do them then. But what they are saying now is that they will do them as soon as they get back into office.
The former minister of agriculture pointed out all the problems. He had the problem of the eastern grain feeders completely analysed but now he criticizes the present government because they have not done anything in the last six or seven months although he had the problem completely analysed, and had the solution available.
What about crop insurance in Alberta? What does your Social Credit government think about that?

There are a lot of mumblings over here, but these members will have plenty of time to talk and say what they want to say before 10.30 tonight. P.F.A.A. has been in effect in western Canada for the last 20 years, and we want it to be abundantly clear that we believe it has been a truly beneficial program for that area. It has been in effect for more than 20 years and I have heard some rumours that the present Minister of Agriculture is disposed to cut the program down a little. If it is true that he is thinking along these lines I suggest that he take a long, hard look at the large area of western Canada that has received a great deal of benefit, with a resulting stabilization of the agricultural economy in that area. In some areas it has applied in cases of drought, but we have also seen very beneficial results as a result of this program in cases of freezing, hail, flooding, early snow and so on. The farmers of western Canada are paying large premiums toward this program. In fact, I think they pay more than 50 per cent of the cost with the exception of the farmers of Saskatchewan. Therefore I suggest to the minister that if he has any idea of cutting down on the P.F.A.A. program he should reconsider the matter.
So far as crop insurance is concerned, we are pleased to hear that the government is now prepared to move into insuring some of the residual risks. I have a very few minutes left, Mr. Chairman, and I am afraid I would not have much success if I were to ask for additional time, so I had better get on with my remarks.
With regard to the matter of an eastern feed grain purchasing board, as it has been called, we agree partially with what the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has said, and I understood from the minister that the government intends to adopt this program. As I said, we agree partially but we do not believe it goes far enough. The submission of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture requests that such a board be set up only in an

Supply-Agriculture
advisory capacity. However, because of the problems that have been placed before the committee by members from these areas of Canada, we believe that we should have an eastern feed grain purchasing board with credit available to it so that it can go to western Canada and buy grain from the Canadian wheat board or in Ontario, or in any event in whatever place it can make the best deal at the most seasonable time of the year.
We are pleased that the government has appropriated $1 million to pay for the storage charges for this winter. We realize this has been helpful in moving a far larger volume of grain into position in eastern Canada. However, in order to solve the problem we think it would be well to have a separate entity that would be charged with the responsibility of buying feed grain at the best possible price. We believe it should be given credit for that purpose, so that it could then move large quantities of grain into position when the seaway is opened, and in fact do for the eastern feeders exactly what the Canadian wheat board is doing for the western producers. We do not believe it should be a branch of the Canadian wheat board, because there would be a conflict of interest. Such a board should be set up, provided with credit and given all the necessary powers it needs to do the job effectively. In our view it should deal with the Canadian wheat board as much as possible so that responsibility would fall on both bodies to see that the job was done.
In closing I want to say a few words about the matter of scrapie. There is a bit of apprehension amongst sheep breeders across the country as to this matter. I did revise my question on the order paper and I would urge the minister and his department to give me a complete and comprehensive answer. I revised the wording of question No. 1,730 so that we could look into this matter.
There is one other point I should like to mention, Mr. Chairman. We do not believe the small amount the federal government is contributing to the veterinary college in western Canada is in keeping with the responsibility the federal government has. The minister admitted the federal Department of Agriculture employs about 25 per cent of these veterinarians in Canada. Apparently, on this basis, they are willing to pay 25 per cent of the capital cost of this college. As a matter of fact, the $625,000 does not even meet the 25 per cent share. However, there are also operating costs and they are going to be substantial over a number of years. We think the federal government, through the health of animals branch, has a responsibility to pay some of the operating costs for training these veterinarians.

In closing, Mr. Chairman, I just want to say we feel the minister should change his attitude concerning a number of things. These debates in this house are not a waste of time. He should move rapidly to set up an eastern feed grain purchasing board. If he will do a number of these things that we suggest, we wish him well.

Mr. Chairman, let me first of all congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for his report. I think this report will give us an opportunity to discuss our problems-I was going to say to leave the western provinces for the eastern provinces.
Since this debate started, we have been hearing about the west and its wheat, for which I hasten to say I am very happy for the western farmers. But when you think that Quebec and Ontario are the provinces where agriculture is the major industry in Canada, and that when farming problems are raised in this house, seven eighths of the discussion are concerned with the western provinces, it seems to me that either the western members defend their cause with too much zeal or the eastern members do not show enough concern to safeguard the interests of their provinces in that regard. In fact, when looking over the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, I note that more than 50 per cent of that budget is allocated to western provinces:
Production and marketing branch-
Freight assistance on western feed grains, $18,500,000.
Board of grain commissioners-
Canadian government elevators, $1,529,000;
Salaries of the commissioners, $42,000;
Administration, $173,000;
Inspection and weighing of grain and related services, $4,656,000;
Under the heading "Land rehabilitation, irrigation and water storage projects", the western provinces are much more favoured than the eastern provinces. The province of Quebec particularly does not get a single dollar for its irrigation projects, while western provinces receive over $33 million for drainage.
Under the heading of "Special estimates", there is an amount of $785,000 concerning the Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration and for the payments in respect of projects and programs under the Agriculture Rehabili-tion and Development Act, the western provinces receive $7 million. For administration, operation and maintenance, $157,000. For payments in connection with the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, $900,000, etc.
Besides that, we find payment of carrying costs of temporary wheat reserves, $41,524.

That goes to show that the western provinces are well treated in parliament.
When I look at those figures, I am tempted to think of the situation in Canada 50 years ago. At that time, the provinces of Quebec and Ontario were considered as the granary of Canada, while the western provinces were thought of as being poor lands, in need of development. Today, we spend all our savings for these provinces, which by the way, deserve it. We levy taxes on our people so as to develop these marvelous prairies of ours. I invite today our western fellow Canadians to show themselves duly grateful.
Before approving these estimates, our group would like to point out to the government three items which interest us most of all: the Farm Credit Corporation-comprising ARDA-the loans to farmers, the department of agriculture for the east and seed grains.
I suppose we cannot find fault with the amount of money the present government has made available to all Canadian farmers. After increasing the amounts paid during the past years, the present government certainly registered a point in favour of the Canadian farmers, and I avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate the minister for the implementation of ARDA, which has been in existence for several years but which has just started to be used in the province of Quebec.
The aim of ARDA, as the minister indicated, is to help the underdeveloped areas. I feel this act is misunderstood in Quebec. The main problem is draining, and for a year every effort has been made to deal more particularly with tree planting. There is a field in which I was in a position last summer to witness the government activity, and it is the blueberry fields. It is very well to look after the blueberry fields, but I believe draining has priority on tree planting, because draining accounts for 50 per cent in my area. There is only 50 per cent of the land which is properly drained.
A better draining of our lands should be put into effect in order to return those lands to farming. And I believe we shall pursue the aim of ARDA only in approaching with greater zeal that vital point, the draining of our soil.
Here I wish to make my meaning perfectly plain by saying that the prime work should first be done in Quebec, and that is why we are trying, with the provincial government's influence, to get what western people have received and to have our lands drained, so that our farmers can return them to farming. However, the government does not help farmers enough. In fact, when we look at the federal budget, we are inclined to feel sorry
Supply-Agriculture
for the minister. Yet, when we realize that the most important department is the Department of Agriculture and that only 2.7 per cent of the total estimates is intended for agriculture, we feel that there is some unbalance here which is hard to understand, and I want to remind the minister of that fact, because it is far too little for Quebec.
But there is another point which remains difficult to understand, Mr. Chairman, and that is the way those amounts are distributed among the provinces.
Here, I do not know whether I should address myself to the government or simply to the Department of Agriculture or to the minister himself, who cannot seem to find the time to go and see at least once what is going on in Quebec.
I would advise him at least to read the reports of the Farm Credit Corporation. Then, by merely reading the data contained therein, he might realize that something is not running true in my province.
The other day I heard the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) boast about the fact that, in 1962, the Conservative government had granted 804 loans, as against 109 in 1961.
When I look at the amount of loans granted in the other provinces, compared to the urgent and ever-increasing needs of the province of Quebec, I come to the conclusion that neither of the old line party governments can pride itself in having given the lion's share to Quebec's agriculture.
And to think that the province of Quebec is now in the worst state of stagnation as far as agriculture is concerned and that it is given, with regard to its population, the least assistance.
I can see that in the past, when exclusive legislation had to be enacted for the western provinces, the governments did not hesitate and passed it in order to benefit these provinces. They did right. Now it is the turn of the province of Quebec to need specific legislation in order to revive its agriculture. Is she going to be denied that legislation any longer?
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the minister make a special study about federal loans granted to the province of Quebec.
At first it might be enough for the minister to improve the staff of the Farm Credit Corporation in the province of Quebec, for I am afraid that the problem lies with the staff which is satisfied to administer rigidly the present legislation because it lacks the ability needed to interpret this legislation, which is too broad, and adapt it to each region, each farmer.

Supp ly-A griculture
As a matter erf fact, I have been told many times by loan inspectors from the Farm Credit Corporation that the act was not precise enough, clear enough or not suited to our regions.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that it would be worth it to have an investigation made in the field by the department in order to find out what is wrong with the legislation and the considerable harm all this is doing to our farmers in need.
I ask the minister to carry out a serious investigation to see what is going wrong in the province of Quebec.
I shall give you an example of the situation in my own area. Our farmers have an urgent need of at least 2,000 federal loans and we succeeded in obtaining only about a hundred this year. This means that 1,900 farmers will not get the money they need to resume work on their farms or to put back under cultivation 40 per cent of our farms which have been waiting only for the necessary manpower for the last 10 or 15 years.
Mr. Chairman, our farms cannot wait any longer, our farmers are forced to leave their farms for the cities. Is it because the legislation is not suited to eastern Canada or is it because the people responsible for its implementation are not able to interpret it? I leave it to you to judge.
It may also be that serious research on the part of the minister would help him to realize the need for an eastern department. This famous department has been promised us for a long time. First, in the speech from the throne, then on the order paper, where it stayed for a while third on the list, to drop almost into oblivion these last months since it is now eleventh on the list.
Yet, we had always cherished the hope that we would have it by 1963; but our hopes were dashed a few days ago when the government announced that we would get it in 1964.
We are somewhat puzzled by all that and we wonder whether this government is responsible. If it were, it would indeed have introduced the various pieces of legislation in order of importance; and since in my opinion agriculture is of prime importance all over Canada, all other matters must give precedence to it. However, it is not at all what we have seen.
Under the existing system, I said and I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that only a department of agriculture for eastern Canada will make it possible to have a well balanced and economical agriculture from coast to coast. We know that from experience. When we had the department of agriculture in eastern Canada, the western provinces were on the verge of bankruptcy. But now it is in western Canada,

and the eastern provinces have a precarious existence. So the only solution is to set up a department of agriculture for the east. And the sooner the better. Pressure is certainly not lacking. I have here an article which appeared in the December 2 issue of Le Droit under the following title:
Appointment requested of a second minister of agriculture for eastern Canada.
The article reads as follows:
The "Meuniers du Quebec Inc." requested the federal government, Friday evening, to carry out without delay its promise to appoint a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada who would enjoy the same rights and privileges of the present Minister of Agriculture.
And further on:
Ottawa was finally urged not to apply next April a first. 4 per cent portion of the Gordon tax on building materials and equipment in order to further the growth of farm production, etc.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that we are now facing facts. Must we wait a long time yet? I think the limit is reached, and if the present Minister of Agriculture does not deal very seriously with this problem and if the government does not organize the business of the house so that this legislation will be presented soon, I am of the opinion that farming, in the province of Quebec, is a long way from reaching new heights.
But outside of the two problems I just mentioned, there is a third one the solution of which can wait no longer, and it is a problem which can be solved by the present Minister of Agriculture.
On October 18, 1963, representatives of the catholic farmers' union and of the federated co-operative of the province of Quebec met our group to set forth their grievances, so as to enable us to relay their representations to this house.
We have already spent many hours listening to the evidence presented by representatives of various organizations concerning feed grains. There is an unaccountable price spread between producers and consumers and it is our duty to find out the truth about the department and so as to bridge the gap between western and eastern farmers.
Several boards have appeared before the committee on agriculture in the past few days. There is no point in enumerating all of them but I think their representatives would like us to find, concerning the problem of feed grains, a solution which would be satisfactory to everyone.
It is urgent for parliament to give serious consideration to that problem which is several years old but is getting worse all the time and gives rise to willful disagreement.

In fact, we can delay no longer the solution of a problem which is threatening the whole agricultural economy.
In the fine brief they submitted, the U.C.C. and the co-operative federee stress the two major problems we must settle to balance the economy of the eastern and western parts of our country.
Right from the start, it strikes you that neither the west nor the east and even less the province of Quebec are to blame for this extraordinary situation which spoils the relations between western Canada and the eastern provinces.
On the contrary, if you examine the situation more closely, you will be pleased to notice that western farmers like their eastern counterparts strive for the same ideal-that of achieving a better standard of living for each group and that they sincerely wish to get along together. However, a wall just like the Berlin wall has gone up, and it prevents the peace-makers from being heard.
If the good will of farmers is not lacking, why can a solution not be found? Where does the situation referred to exist? It is precisely this vital question that I intend to answer.
In this case, Mr. Chairman, I suspect that a dictatorship is being exerted by an organization enjoying special favours from governments, so as to wield its powers without fear of being ousted.
The prairie provinces are recognized as the best grain producers. The climate, the soil and the geographic location are so many factors which have made the prairie provinces the granary of Canada, enabling them to exert their influence even on world markets. On the other hand, eastern provinces are recognized for the variety of their agricultural production which goes from maple syrup to market-gardening crops and cattle.
It would merely be logical that these two regions, the east as well as the west, be given the necessary scope, and I would even say enjoy the necessary assistance, from the governments to launch into their own production.
We all know that to be in a position to produce, the farmer needs a minimum cost price. Consequently, the catholic farmers' union stresses in its brief that the eastern farmer should be in a position to earn his living with his products
We do not wish the same mistakes to be repeated as when western farmers were being paid to refrain from producing wheat or again not long ago, when the Minister of Agriculture abolished the 25 cents premium per hundred pounds of milk and went so far as to ask the Quebec milk producers to reduce their production, at a time when so
Supply-Agriculture
many Quebec families do not have enough milk, and that is particularly true in our
schools.
The purpose of our inquiry today is therefore to find who is responsible for this inconceivable inconsistency shown by a government which dares to claim it is still democratic.
On one side, we have people who want one thing only: to produce wheat, and on the other side, we have people who need wheat and cannot buy it because its price is exorbitant.
Where is the key to this mystery?
Mr. Chairman, we are fighting the very cancer of our farm economy, and it is that same cancer which affects every sector of our national economy. In every field, industrial, monetary and so on, the evil always comes from faulty distribution.
The present formula is all for one and nothing for the others. The great master of our economy is still the trust.
Mr. Chairman, when you think that the western producer gets only 55 cents per bushel of grain, for which the eastern consumer must pay up to $1.50, that is fantastic. So there is not only the case of other financiers even more brazen who, with a $10 deposit, succeed in borrowing $100, just like the chartered banks.
As a matter of fact, if you push your inquiries further, you will find that all the western wheat is delivered to the great lakes by the Canadian wheat board, which sets the price according to the price paid to the western farmers, plus the transportation costs which are borne by those same farmers. I think also that the grants paid by the governments for the transportation and storage of grain help maintain the price of grain at a more reasonable level today.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member for Roberval, but his time is up.

Mr. Chairman, I will be very brief because none of us on this side wants to hold up the minister's estimates. In fact, we are prepared to co-operate to the extent that I will probably be the last speaker as far as we are concerned, if we get the cooperation we anticipate the minister will give us. As he knows, a matter has arisen under the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which is to be referred to the committee on privileges and elections. The minister has received a request from the clerk of that committee to appear before it tomorrow morning. If the minister can give us the assurance that he will be with us

Supply*-Agriculture
tomorrow morning, then I will be quite happy and conclude my remarks at this point.

I am very sorry but I cannot give that commitment. I have a speaking engagement at the annual meeting of the farm union in Alberta which I am committed to, and have been for some time. But I will be back and am quite prepared to meet the committee on Saturday morning.

This presents a problem. The committee has not decided to meet on Saturday and it is not usual for committees of the house to sit on a Saturday. Therefore Saturday is not a suitable date. The reason I raise the matter at this time is because when the minister was informed that he was requested to appear before the committee he replied to the clerk that he was unable to do so. Since that time we have heard second hand, through the hon. member for Carleton, the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand and the hon. member for York-Scarborough, of different commitments. Some mentioned Wednesday, some Tuesday and now it is Saturday. The request was sent to the minister to appear on Friday.
We are perfectly agreeable to working out some arrangement in co-operation with the minister. I am not suggesting for a moment that this is what he has in mind, but what we fear is that he might not appear before the committee at all before this session is over unless we get some commitment from him this evening. The committee meets at nine o'clock tomorrow morning. If the minister was there his evidence could be taken within an hour, and then he could get off to Calgary and meet his commitment there.

I am quite prepared to meet the
committee; as a matter of fact I welcome the opportunity. I have stated my problem, and would be quite prepared to meet the committee at nine o'clock on Friday evening, or Saturday morning, or seven o'clock Monday morning, or Tuesday morning or Wednesday morning-any one of these mornings. Next week the ten ministers of agriculture are to be here and we have a conference starting on Monday, and running Tuesday and Wednesday, so it will be difficult for me to appear any time after nine o'clock. However, as I say, I am quite prepared to meet the committee at seven in the morning.

That is fine. If the minister is prepared to meet the committee at nine o'clock tomorrow evening and is agreeable to be the first witness to be examined on that committee, then we are quite happy on this side.
God willing, I will do that.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak perhaps I could comment on some remarks made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I could not help but think that perhaps he was preaching for a call. Whether that call was to be next minister of agriculture in a Liberal government I am not sure, but that thought did run through my mind as he talked on and on, on a Liberal theme, about farm machinery being the main trouble with agriculture generally. I questioned him as to where his party stood on communist countries buying Canadian wheat. Not only did he not have time to deal with the question at that moment, but he failed to deal with it at all. He failed to deal with his party's viewpoint on that crucial issue in the last two elections. Why did he fail to do that? The only thought which came to my mind was that perhaps he was going to cross the floor of the house and no longer remain with his present party.
The hon. member talked about ARDA and how vague it was. He did not say that it has not worked very well in Alberta, because the government of Alberta has not made any real, concentrated effort to make it work or to see that it would work. The reason is that they are afraid to spend some of the money they have in their oil rich treasury and put it back into the basic industry of the country. The basic industry of Alberta is still agriculture, but we are still fighting to see that some share of their provincial money goes back to the land; but it is a hard fight in that province.
The hon. member also talked about the study on the Saskatchewan and Nelson rivers basin, which includes the Red Deer river project, a very vital project to central Alberta reaching down as far as his own constituency. According to him, no more studies were needed in this regard. He said he had a study in his own office, but he did not say what year it was. I have one too. In fact, there have been studies ever since the William Peers project in 1918, as well as 1928 and 1942. I do not know which study he has but we are now in 1963. We now have the Alberta government stingily not wanting to go ahead with any study. They have resisted co-operation with the prairie provinces water board? Why? Because here again they have been reluctant to spend some of their money, received from wealth resources below the surface on the land itself, to replenish and develop the basic industry of agriculture.
Oh, oh.

This wisecracking at the other end of the chamber reminds me of an old saying that wisecrackers rarely gather wisdom. The hon. member talked

about community pastures and the greater need for them throughout Canada. What is the attitude of the Alberta government in this regard? There has been no federal participation in community pastures within the provinces; that is what they tell us in Alberta. The province from which the hon. member comes is a Social Credit province, and he has the gall to get up in this house and say that he wants further action on community pastures by the federal government, when the federal government itself is not allowed to enter the province in this respect. There are some 70 new community pastures which have sprung up in the last four or five years in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, but not one in Alberta-except the one brought about by a severe drought. We were also able to secure a large part of the Suffield experimental station as a sort of community pasture, but on a limited basis. But this was done through the Department of National Defence. Though his remarks were interesting, he said very little. He did not take into account, in the course of his observations, the thinking of the federal Social Credit party with regard to sales to Russia, or the thinking of the provincial party, for that matter. The only conclusion I can reach is that he was preaching for a call-that he was expecting to become the next minister of agriculture in the Liberal party. This has been suggested by a learned journalist whom we have among us, namely the hon. member for Port Arthur. Maybe the hon. member for Port Arthur is right in this regard. Who am I to say?
When I rose to speak tonight I did not intend to deal with the speech made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, but I thought it deserved comment, if only on account of what the hon. member did not say. In speaking tonight, I should like to make it clear I have no axe to grind with the present Minister of Agriculture as a person. I know he has a highly successful record in real estate, as a farmer and as an entrepreneur of most descriptions. He has a reputation in this regard and I respect him for it. But he has failed miserably as a leader of agriculture in this country, and it is in this direction that I want to direct my criticism. He has provided no leadership either to the department, or to Canada, or to the farmers across the country. His speech today was nothing more than a factual report, item by item, on the estimates of the department. There was no review of the future outlook for the Department of Agriculture. No real leadership was shown with regard to the general direction in which we are moving. It is obvious that someone inside the department wrote his speech. It certainly differed greatly from
Supp ly-A griculture
the speech which was made in Chicago some time ago when the hon. gentleman said there were only four members in the Liberal party who knew anything about agriculture. I really did not know whether he was including himself among those four or not, and I wondered who the other three might be. That speech must have been a real eye-opener for the people in Illinois, Montana, and the west, generally.
I looked in the hon. gentleman's speech today for some show of leadership. I tried to discover where the Liberals were going to lead western agriculture and agriculture in Canada generally. I thumbed through a copy of the Liberal promises with regard to agriculture. This is what they said:
A Liberal government will provide continuous, "realistic guidance on the market outlook for different crops and livestock products".
Hear, hear.

I hear members over there pounding their desks. Well, I have several other clippings here. Here is a beauty: "Hays calls for less wheat". That is from the Farm Union of October 2. Was this an example of realistic guidance on the market outlook for different crops? I should like to say a word or two more about this Liberal program because I saw nothing in the speech from the throne or in the remarks of the minister to indicate there was any consideration being given to continuing the ideas they had at the beginning of 1963. What is being forecast for 1964? What can we expect in the next speech from the throne? Here is what they said:
Under a Liberal government, a reorganized industrial development bank will be able to provide long term finance for co-operatives. Improved research services will benefit co-operatives.
I looked for that in the speech from the throne this spring but I never saw anything about it and I have not heard anything about it since. Here is another quotation from the program:
A Liberal government is pledged to increase the return to the farmer from wheat sold in Canada for human consumption.
Well, I see no evidence that this is being done. Then again, there was the $2 a bushel wheat, and there was the two price system. The program is specific about this. The Prime Minister, speaking in Saskatoon on March 6, said:
This policy (two price system for wheat) will be accompanied by a consumer subsidy so that there will be no rise in the price of bread.
No more has been heard about that. Another change forecast in that program was the introduction of deficiency payments on a quarterly basis for oats and barley and a wide

Sup p ly-A griculture
range of agricultural products. I would point out to the committee that only the other day the minister announced a policy with regard to eggs. Did he say payments were to be made on a quarterly basis? No, he did not. This, like the rest of this program, has been completely forgotten. Even the few ideas which the Liberals might have been able to grasp as possible solutions for some of the difficulties in which agriculture now finds itself, have been forgotten, too. I could read on but I see I should lose too much time if I got worked up over these broken promises. No wonder the party opposite includes so few members from the rural areas of Canada. No wonder the Liberal party is represented by only four members who know anything about agriculture. It is because they have advocated this false Liberal program over the years.
Farmers and other Canadians want leadership from a minister of agriculture. They want a future to which they can look forward. The minister talked about ARDA. What has happened to ARDA since the program became the responsibility of the present government? It has become an almost completely ineffective piece of legislation. The sum of $4 million has been made available to it, the minister has told us, though $50 million was made available by the previous government over a three year period. The hon. gentleman talked about farm credit and the leadership which has been provided in this regard. The Liberal program says:
Farmers who wish to switch from dairying to other enterprises to which their farms are better suited, will be encouraged in the Liberal plan by credit and assistance specifically adapted to this purpose.
Have we heard anything about this promise since? No. The minister mentioned farm credit a while ago, but that is all. The operations of the stabilization board remain unchanged. Perhaps the board needs some modernization. That is why amendments to acts are introduced.
The hon. gentleman spoke of the dairy industry. Well, the butter subsidy is still the same only we are able, now, to balance our production against our consumption as a result of a Conservative program for paying a subsidy to butter consumers which has brought about an increase in consumption. Certainly, there is a problem in connection with eastern feed grain. We have been studying it for three or four days now. Provisional pricing may and I think will provide a benefit. But this was already designed before, under our announced policy for legislation in the house. The storage charges on grain are going to be paid. This is similar to what we had promised we were going to do. The minister

said that an agency would be assigned to look after this matter, but the agency would have no teeth in it. It is a rather useless agency if that is all it is going to be.
In an earlier speech he made in the house he talked about farm machinery and said there must be depots and renting and pools. Any western farmer who is depending for his whole livelihood on 7,000 or 8,000 bushels of grain that must be harvested wants his own combine so he can get out and harvest it. Back in the early 'forties a lot of custom combining was done, but the trend is away from that today. It may go back to it but I do not think it will. As for renting and pools, I found renting to be rather expensive. I am in several machinery pools with some of my neighbours. With certain types of inexpensive machines which can be used at any time of the season pools will work all right. But a tractor represents 50 per cent of the farm machinery cost of any given farmer and a tractor and combine are needed if one is to engage in the farming business in a full time way at all. No pool will provide any real solution to that. When the minister talked about this a while ago I wonder whether he had read the report of the committee on agriculture set up to study that question some time ago.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
I am sorry but I am running out of time.
I'll say you are.

You can ask me a
question at the end of my speech. We have heard a lot of talk about why the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners were switched from the Department of Agriculture back to the Department of Trade and Commerce. The farmers wondered why. The reason is obvious. The Minister of Agriculture had something to say on June 22, 1963, which indicates the reason. He was referring to the China wheat sale and he said:
That comes under the trade and commerce department now, and I know little about It.
"I know little about it". We never had such a barefaced admission of the facts before. Of course, he was a new minister then. "I know little about it". This was obvious to many western farmers and to many people throughout Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a former deputy minister of the department. The Minister of Agriculture was appointed by the Prime Minister, and as the Minister of Agriculture knew little about the subject it was natural to switch these boards back, not for the benefit of the producers but for the benefit of the Liberal party. That is

why it was done. It is obvious, and most Canadians recognize this fact now.
The Minister of Agriculture made a tour of Russia. What did he say about wheat over there? This was before the gigantic wheat deal with that country. What did he say? He never said anything. He did not come back and say, "I saw a poor crop over there".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: You do not understand Russian anyway.

You can look out the train window and see whether the crop is going to go five bushels to the acre or 40 bushels. The minister came back and said: "We can sell a lot more purebred Canadian beef over there".
More bull.

Well, perhaps so. We are looking, and I mean the Canadian public, for leadership in the Department of Agriculture. Here is what the Ottawa Journal said yesterday in referring to the whole hoax of the 60 days of decision of the present government. The editorial refers to the promise of two ministers of agriculture and goes on to say:
It can hardly be said that there is even one minister.
That is a shocking statement to appear in a Canadian paper. That is a shocking statement to make about the primary industry of this country. We can hardly say we even have one. That is in direct contrast to what the situation was back in 1962 and 1961. Everybody in Canada knew then that we had a minister of agriculture, and everybody was proud of that minister of agriculture.
We hear a lot about leadership and the minister's position. At a meeting of the farmers union in Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, the minister said:
I would be irresponsible if I didn't urge farmers to examine the question of wheat output-
The heading of the article in the October Union Farmer is "Hays Calls for Less Wheat". The article goes on to say that the minister said the government would do all it could to investigate the problem. We wanted leadership. We wanted guidance.
That is what you need, leadership.

This is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to say about the same problem on August 12, 1963 at Edmonton, as found in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix:
Trade minister Mitchell Sharp stressed the need to reduce wheat acreage and production in favour of more barley and oats production.
Supply-Agriculture
We all remember that famous speech. Is this realistic guidance to the farmers of Canada as to what they are to do and what they are to produce? Certainly it is a shortsighted attitude on the part of two ministers of the cabinet, and they took it not because of their knowledge of the subject but because they were jealous of the record established by the former minister and wanted to cut it down to their size, or below their size if at all possible. That is why they took that attitude.
We have heard some talk today about a veterinary college in western Canada and the minister's offer of 25 per cent or $625,000. I read an editorial in the Canadian Cattleman which condemned the minister for being so stingy. It pointed out that the federal government will spend $1 million to build a vocational training school. They have in Drum-heller, Stettler and many other places throughout Alberta and Canada generally. But they will only put up $625,000 for a veterinary college when the federal government is importing veterinarians into this country. Is this logical? When we are importing veterinarians from Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand is this logical? The minister wrote a very nice letter to the editor of the Canadian Cattleman and explained that he wanted to suck in the provincial governments, and he felt that if he put up enough bait one of them would grab it because he knew they were all eager to have it. With regard to the Department of Agriculture spending money, I would point out that the minister said, as reported in the Regina Leader-Post of June 28, 1963:
There would be nothing wrong with spending a lot more on agriculture in this country.
The minister knew he could suck in the province of Saskatchewan on a veterinary college because they wanted to get it before it went to the proper place, Alberta, where most of the cattle are, and the minister was quite successful. Another Social Credit Albertan is pounding his desk, but how he can do that I do not know when the province of Alberta, which is so wealthy from oil and gas, is so stingy with regard to spending money on the basic industry of that province.
I am going to have to slow up a little perhaps, and try to get across the theme of my remarks. If the Prime Minister does not choose somebody more capable of providing leadership for agriculture, and the present minister is allowed to continue to wander and squander throughout the department and throughout Canada, then I want to make a few suggestions in the hope that if he is left in that department he will heed the call of Canadians generally, and of the agriculture

Supply-Agriculture
industry, for a strong minister of agriculture, a minister with foresight and leadership.
At the beginning of the minister's term of office I was reluctant, as the record will prove, to ask him questions and to press him because I knew he was a new minister. I also know he is a capable businessman in his own personal business. But I want him to take hold, to take an interest and to go to work in this department, if he is capable of providing leadership.
In the early days of the session, there was a bit of comment concerning some of the replies the minister made in the house. If the minister was not in his seat, we pointed this out to hon. members. If he happened to be away selling cattle, we gently nudged him and said, "Now, Harry, you have a new job; you have to drop this cattle selling and assume a more important role in Canadian life." However, the minister continued his efforts on behalf of a few of my learned colleagues, like Dr. Rynard and others who are in the cattle industry and who sell purebred cattle.
If one takes a certain look at what this government has done during 200 days in office, he must conclude it is time the Prime Minister took a look at this department. We have looked at all the departments. We have gone through finance, post office, health and welfare and so on. Now, let us look at the basic industry of this country, agriculture. It is still the backbone of the country. All I am asking is that we take a look at this department. The minister must ask himself, "Do I want to be minister? Do I want to bring in new programs? Do I want to explain those programs in this parliament or do I want to continue travelling across Canada as an auctioneer for cattle breeders?" If he does continue this practice, he is neglecting his official duties.
The Toronto Globe and Mail has commented on this situation more than once. They even suggested that there was talk of having two ministers, but we have not seen the second one. We rarely see the first. Perhaps we need a third. Surely, 200 days is sufficient time for the minister to find himself and take hold of his duties.
The Ottawa Journal had this to say:
He will say, naturally, that cabinet ministers often appear on ceremonial occasions to give their blessings to buildings, fairs and other worth-while projects. The trouble with Mr. Hays is that he wants to participate rather than visit. If he were invited to lay a cornerstone we fear that he would keep the trowel and put up the whole wall.
This shows the man has energy, and I want him to use it for the benefit of the whole of Canadian agriculture, and not a special group he seems to prefer. I suggest that unless the Minister of Agriculture spends some time in

the House of Commons and in his department^ gets to know his department, becomes aware of the feeling of the average Canadian farmer,, then he should spend all of his time at auctions. At one time, the minister boastfully stated, in speaking about agriculture in Alberta, that he had 5,000 acres of land, so many hired hands, trucks and so on. This does not entitle him to boast about his personal efforts in the field of agriculture. He is now the minister looking after the welfare of a vast number of farmers who do not have that same financial backing, and perhaps are in need of some financial backing.
It may be that some of my friends on the other side of the house will think I am being a little rough on their lovable friend, Harry. I am doing this for the explicit purpose of trying to direct his attention back to the Department of Agriculture, if it ever was on the department, for the benefit of farmers generally throughout Canada. Frankly, the minister must realize that he is no longer in the position of an athlete in the prime of life. He is rather like a hockey or baseball player reaching the end of his career but still trying to continue. The minister has now been called upon to accept a higher role in the affairs of Canada. He must meet that challenge that is presented to him. He must turn his mind away from his chosen line of business and direct his attention to the new aspect that confronts him. He must show a greater amount of leadership, a greater amount of foresight in his efforts to raise the standard of living of farmers throughout Canada.
May I ask the hon. member a simple question? Why does the hon. member spend so much time complaining, when all the western farmers are so happy after the record wheat sale we had this year?

I could have dealt with wheat sales. I imagine you are going to give me time to deal with this question, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Medicine Hat suggested something along the same line. I may point out that I asked the members of the wheat board about wheat sales in the committee the other day. I asked what government provided the first credit wheat sales, and they frankly admitted that before the first China wheat sale there had never been any other wheat sale like it. No other government had attempted to put up that kind of credit for the sale of wheat. This sale established a pattern. We in the west are proud of it.
I was a member in those days when wheat sales were not being made, and I recall the great difficulties. We urged the cabinet at that time to consider the question of credit sales. For years, the farm unions had been crying

lor this type of thing. We went ahead and did it. The farmers in western Canada know about wheat sales and they are happy with this program. They wanted it years ago, and now that it has been established it is starting to bear fruit. It bore more fruit last year and is continuing to bear fruit this year. The Eormer minister of agriculture, the Hon. Alvin Hamilton, told them to go out and grow all the wheat they could and he would sell it. He was quite sure of the market outlook at that time. Away back as far as February, 1963, he forecast record wheat sales for this year. This is nothing new to the farmers. They accepted this and they are grateful to the Minister of Trade and Commerce for continuing the pattern we established.
We want further leadership on many of the other agricultural problems, such as credit. I could go into these problems at length, but I realize, Mr. Chairman, you have been patient in allowing me to answer this question.

I feel very humble indeed, after listening to my colleagues talk about the huge tractors required, and the great horsepower required, to operate their farms. I rise to speak, Mr. Chairman, only as a rancher who has a five horsepower lawn-mower. I might say also that I would not attempt to compete with the hon. gentleman who has taken his seat, so far as lung power is concerned.
Listening to these debates on agriculture throughout the years makes one realize that there have been a number of interesting personalities who have been ministers of agriculture from western Canada. We all remember the Hon. W. R. Motherwell, who I think was respected by all regardless of party; the late Hon. James Gardiner who, while we differed very sharply, was recognized as a fighter, particularly for prairie agriculture. Then, we had the Hon. Douglas Harkness who, while he was very conscientious and sincere, I always felt was more at home on the parade ground than in the village hall. Then, we had the Hon. Alvin Hamilton, who was an auctioneer of ideas. He was a very conscientious minister and left some worth-while policies behind him which I trust the present government will do something to continue and improve.
Now Mr. Chairman, I come to the present Minister of Agriculture. I cannot help commenting, as I sit in the house on this side and watch his cherubic expression, regardless of statements being made by various members of the opposition, that he is an auctioneer of livestock. We have had two very famous speeches by ministers this session, two that will probably go down in history. The first was made by the Minister without Portfolio, more correctly termed the minister
Supply-Agriculture
still in waiting. He made a very well organized, fruitful and, I thought, thoughtful speech. I read the text in one of the agricultural magazines. I can well imagine his getting the assistance of the officials and members of the profession that he knows; possibly even his good wife, because it was obvious after you read the speech that he was preaching for a call.
I intended, Mr. Chairman, to deal with another aspect of agricultural policy this evening, but I feel that owing to the development of the debate and these two famous speeches, they should be dealt with. I am going to deal with the speech the Minister of Agriculture made to the farmers club in Chicago on December 2. I might explain that I understand the farmers club in Chicago is like the members of the Rideau club in stetson hats. Anyway, the minister is almost unknown in the interior of British Columbia. I have had many inquiries and letters asking me, "What does he look like? How does he think?"
Does he?

"How does he talk? What does he say?" Mr. Chairman, I am going to let him speak for himself. This will save me a great deal of correspondence and I think it is worth while letting the people of Canada know how the minister thinks, because if you size up how the minister thinks you get some idea of what Liberal agricultural policy is.
This famous speech in Chicago was given on the same day that the hon. member for Red Currant-
Oh, oh.

-Swift Current-Maple Creek rose on a question of privilege. The committee will remember that the minister's absence was noted, as usual, and the Prime Minister rose and explained that he was away on official business. I shall deal with the official business in a few minutes. His speech was taped; parts of it have been given on the radio and it has whetted the appetite of thousands for more. It is unique. It is unusual, and I am sure when the members of this house have heard it they will say it is a fantastic speech. It is a speech that deals with his family tree; that deals with his rise -his Horatio Alger rise from a farm boy to a position of prestige and importance in the federal government; that deals with his philosophy of life and then deals with Liberal agricultural policy. I think we owe it to the members of this house and to the nation to let them know how the minister thinks. I have a text of the speech here taken from the tape recording:

Supp ly-A gricu Iture
Speech by the Hon. Harry Hays, Minister of Agriculture, to the Chicago farmers club, December 2, 1963.
This is an authorized and authentic copy.
When it was suggested to me that I should come and speak to the Chicago farmers club, I decided that I wanted to do that job. I have the kind of Prime Minister who allows me to come down here-
Wasn't that kind of him?
-and I understand that I am the first of his ministers who has had the privilege of speaking in Chicago. In any case, I am elated to be here. Dr. Wilson, in introducing me, was pretty kind to me because generally I've been in trouble all my life-
That is an understatement, if ever there was one.
Oh, oh.

His speech continues:
To be the Minister of Agriculture, to be the mayor of a city, to be the auctioneer of a good sale, or of a poor sale, you have to be a bit of an optimist and to show you how optimistic I am about the problems of the farmers and that sort of thing I'd like to tell you a story about an uncle of mine.
This is very closely related to agriculture. You can see the minister was on official business.
I live in Alberta, which is north of the state of Montana. And our country is much the same as some parts of Montana. And we have there a government called a Social Credit government, which has turned into a very conservative republican government.
There is a point I want to raise here, Mr. Chairman. This has caused a great deal of concern. Is the minister now co-operating with the hon. member for Lotbiniere in a campaign against Her Majesty? I hope the minister explains this when he replies later on in the debate, because it is causing concern.
During the depression time, they put a moratorium on interest payments so that the farmer might be able to pay his debts. They wouldn't let anybody foreclose.
It sounds as if the minister was a bit disappointed himself.
But I had an uncle who lived in a small town where I was born, north of Calgary, who had guaranteed a couple of million dollars worth of loans. He had guaranteed the interest, so you can see what happened to him during the depression- the interest he had to pay dissipated his complete fortune.
Well, he had a heart at least:
We had a little hotel about a half mile from the cemetery.
A good place.
And we lived about four miles out of town, but he decided when this took place that he would go down to the hotel every morning to try and drink the beer faster than they could make it. He did this for 20 years. Every morning he was the first fellow there and every night he was the last guy to go home. Of course he didn't

have much money left and he was the town gossip. Not only did everybody talk about him, but during the day he talked about everybody else.
I have a great deal of respect for this uncle of mine. He was a real champion of mine because he had been very, very successful in the real estate business.
This indicates that the minister's mind is not directed toward agriculture; it is still directed principally toward business.
I remember we had an old postmaster who used to go over and pick up the mail every day when the train came in at one o'clock. He had a two-wheel cart and he'd take it back to the post office and sort the mail every day. You set your clock by him. When he was a very old man, one day he died. And they came down to the beer parlour and someone said to this group where my uncle was partaking that day, "Say, you know Joe King died" My uncle said, "Well, isn't that something".
He left a will and they wanted him to open up the will right away. So, they opened it up and (now remember I told you the cemetery is about a half a mile away from the beer parlour), he said in his will he wanted to be buried eight feet deep.
My uncle looked at it for a minute, and he finally said, "Well I'll tell you what to do. You let them bury old Joe King eight feet deep and when I die you just bury me two feet deep. And on resurrection day I'll be down to the beer parlour before old Joe King is at the cemetery gate".
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: This is the minister who was on federal business.
Why don't you give the figures?

I am glad I am getting encouragement from the minister. I was afraid I was boring him.
At the moment we ship to you something like 500,000 head of beef cattle a year. Now this compares, I think, with about half as much as you get from Australia. I don't know what the figures are and the amount that you receive from Mexico and some of these countries, but this is the comparison and these are the things that we worry about when it looks as though you may cut us off.
And I'll give you these round figures which I think will be of interest to you. The total amount of beef that we ship into the United States in a year represents 5.8 per cent, that is five days of your total consumption. That is all the beef we send in. And the meat that we import represents, although it is a smaller amount, seven days consumption for Canada. Now get these figures because they are pretty important. Although the amounts are different, the amount of meat that we ship into the United States represents a five day supply for you, a bit over five days and a half. The amount that we import in beef products, processed beef, stripped beef and that sort of thing, feeds our people for seven days.
But when we take all of the agricultural products that we ship into the United States, and you are our best customers, it will feed your people for one and a half days. The amount of feed, the amount in dollars, the amount that you ship back to us will feed our people for 29 days.
So you can see how concerned we become sometimes when one segment of the industry says, "Well, we don't like these exports (or imports) coming into our country." We would hope that you would take a look at the whole picture. This is

Supply-Agriculture
a pretty big story to sell, but it's a pretty big thing to us in Canada, when we are in this position. Stop and think about poultry lor instance. We import 35 to your one in Canada; our exports are one part and yours are 35. In cheese it is four to one in your favour. In so far as grain is concerned we don't send much grain in here, but last year we imported from you 35 million bushels of corn, which we were pleased to get.
But here's something we would like you to consider in so far as Canada is concerned. Because we have to live together on this North American continent we're one and the same economy. We are a great storehouse of energy and oil and all of the things that you may need in strategic materials waiting to be used by the North American people. There are certain things in the United States that we must always have, things that we can't grow because geography makes it impossible for us to grow. I mentioned a few of these, for instance cotton. We must have your cotton. We will always need it. We can't grow cotton, we'll need your citrus fruits, oranges, grapefruit; we need your vegetables out of season. We need rice, we need soybeans-
