I am sure, Mr. Chairman, I remember the hon. member for Essex East pleading with the former government to assist the soybeans producers in Ontario.
-we need peanuts. All of these things are agricultural commodities that you people produce that we cannot or never never will produce.
This all adds up to the fact that our economy is a high-cost one, compared with yours because we're north of the 49th parallel and we have to live with the elements. The United States and Canada will always be great trading nations. I was going to mention wheat. We have in Canada 60 million acres of arable land. We farm 5 per cent of Canada-just the small amount of 5 per cent. This 60 million acres hasn't changed in the last 30 years very much.
It won't change very much in the next few years because they are going to drown a lot of land in the Kootenays.
This year we had a bumper crop of wheat. We grew something like 700 million bushels-720 to be exact-which is a record crop. The highest we've ever grown from 27 million acres. And then a small amount of soft wheat which we grew in Ontario, for which you would have to add a couple of million bushels. This grain for the most part, has been marketed as you know. We grew 27 million acres at the expense of a certain amount of acreage that would ordinarily be sown to oats and barley and coarse grains and that sort of thing. But this grain is an expensive proposition for us. So are our beef cattle an expensive proposition for us. So are our dairy products.
This is a very interesting paragraph.
If we in dairy products are going to live or compete with the rest of the world, for instance Argentina or New Zealand or Australia, we will have to change our whole pattern of dairy farming. But I don't say that we will have to change it so far as the cost of fluid milk is concerned. As long as we are shipping fluid milk we will have to produce it the year round.
But we are giving great consideration to educating our people to live with geography. For instance, you can produce a pound of cheese at almost half the amount of money in the summer as you can in the winter.

I would like the minister to explain this, because it almost indicates that you milk the cows in summer and let them dry up in the winter.
Storage facilities have changed and we are taking a long look at some of these problems.
We are also at the moment taking a long look at the high cost of machinery in Canada. We think that if we are going to be producing for world markets, then we must take a look at some of these great problems. Because it doesn't seem right that you should have $40,000 invested in a section that requires $25,000 or $30,000 worth of machinery to operate it. Particularly when you think about the problems we have in Canada. One year we might have a big crop like we had this year and a farmer has 6,000 bushels of wheat on 300 acres. And he hasn't had it marketed and his neighbour has the same thing so he goes out and buys an $8,000 or $9,000 combine. And then the next year he's sitting there with the combine and he got hailed out and his neighbour got hailed out and everybody else. So he's got no place to put the combine. And the third year he got dried out and about that time the old lady ran away with the hired man and he's in a real mess, this fellow.
I suggest that it is not fair to the farm housewife of the prairie provinces to suggest that they are in the practice of running away with the hired man.
These are some of the problems that confront the Canadian farmer, and I'm sure you have the same problem here. Another thing that we're taking a look at is crop disaster. When a man is hailed out, blown out, frozen out, all of these are a great worry to him and we think that we admire some of your crop insurance and we are going to take a long look at this.
We shall be interested in the minister's intentions in regard to that.
When we were in Holland we saw it was costing $2,000 an acre to reclaim land from the sea. And we were told that they were selling this back to the producer at greatly reduced prices and giving him 60 years to pay for it at 3 per cent interest. This will show you the important place the farmer holds in these older countries. The producer of food is the very backbone of their economy.
I agree with the minister there.
Mr. Chairman, I would think that we have the same problems here. We in Canada would like to work very closely with you in agriculture. I suggested the last time I saw your secretary of agriculture, Mr. Freeman, that we would like to ship a little more cheese into the United States. And because we only send in 500,000 pounds and we Import 2 million pounds it looked to me like we had a real good argument. He said "Well, but you have Cheddar cheese". I said to him "I think this is a specialty cheese and I'm going to call it Freeman cheese from now on."
I hope that if he is elected again-
Actually, the secretary of agriculture is appointed over there, not elected-
-we will be able to export more cheese into the United States.
Now, I'm being a little facetious about this, but these are some of the problems that confront us in Canada. We have a great deal of admiration for our friends in the United States, the farmer

particularly, because you have given us the very foundation of our dairy cattle; most of the best ones come from this country.
I differ with the minister over that. The original stock of the Ayrshire herds and the Holsteins came from Scotland, Great Britain and the European countries, and most of the best ones come from this country.
Much of our cereal seed grain comes from this country.
He means the United States, there.
We would like to work closely with you in research also. Our problems will always be the same because it looks as though for quite some time we are going to be producing all agricultural commodities in surplus and so we will be competing in world markets.
The minister has anticipated that we are going to be producing agricultural commodities in surplus for some time. This represents an almost subconscious thinking and I hope the minister explains that statement when he replies.
Nevertheless, we would like to work very closely with you people in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity of speaking to you this afternoon. I would be remiss in my duties if I did not invite you back to Canada. I hope that you will see fit to come to Canada. It has been a real pleasure to be here this afternoon. I only wish I could stay this evening. Thank you very much.
Mr. Chairman, I have put this somewhat unusual speech on the record because I think it will save a lot of members' time explaining what type of man the minister is, how he thinks, how he talks, and what government agricultural policy is. This will enlighten the people of Canada and I trust that when the minister replies later on he will explain some of his ambiguous statements. We expect ambiguous statements from the Secretary of State for External Affairs but not from the Minister of Agriculture. I have always claimed in talking to other hon. members of my group that there is one thing about farmers-you know where they stand. But I tell you at this stage, Mr. Chairman, we do not know where the Minister of Agriculture stands.

Mr. Chairman, the agricultural problems in our area are being seriously considered by a growing number of people in eastern Canada.
It should be said, therefore, that the eastern farmer's lot is receiving the kind attention of many members of this house who have made up their minds to draw plans to improve substantially and without delay the difficult financial situation in which the farmers find themselves.

According to official reports, there would be one area in Canada, the west, where farmers have seen their financial situation gradually improve in recent years, whereas, in the case of eastern farmers, the situation is deteriorating to the point where many are and will be incapable of carrying their burden.
However, thank goodness, solutions are being proposed to prevent the disaster from spreading.
The catholic farmers' union and the federated co-operative of Quebec have always been engaged in promoting and protecting the general interest of agriculture. In the last few months, both associations, which are beneficial and essential to the welfare of farmers, have submitted requests to the proper quarter in order that a sound solution to the problems of their members be found, particularly the problem of the feed grain required by the stock-breeding industry in eastern Canada.
It is easy to see that western farmers, generally speaking, are satisfied at the present time. On the other hand, they do not seem to be too much interested in eastern Canada buyers and to be anxious to inquire about prices paid by customers who are farmers like themselves.
At the present time, we have to pay close to $20 a ton, for instance, for feed grain delivered in Montreal. And it is precisely on that point that we have to co-operate if we want the purposes of the stock-breeders in my region to be achieved. On that matter, the officers of our syndicates and co-operatives have their heart set on attaining our object, which is to participate in the crop abundance in the prairie provinces, in the reasonable and equitable prices obtained by western farmers and finally, allow our stock-breeders in eastern Canada to benefit from a steady and necessary increase.
Thus, since 1941, the federal government grants a freight subsidy for feed grain produced in the prairie provinces and consumed on farms in eastern Canada and in British Columbia.
In Montreal, that subsidy amounts to $5 a ton at the present time. As an average for the whole province, it amounts to some $8 a ton.
That is not a statutory policy. The subsidy is annual and is renewed each year by order in council.
Quebec imports about one million tons of grain and mill feed from western mills, that is 35 or 40 per cent of the requirements. For the fiscal year ended March 1961, Quebec farmers received some $7.7 million under that policy.
On an average, the province of Quebec gets 40 per cent of the total amount paid out by the federal government under that policy-

Supp ly-A griculture
The province of Quebec is a dairy province directed toward grass farming. Its natural environment is quite suited for such direction.
An excellent method of consolidating the Quebec farms is to direct their activities towards those livestock productions in which we are short. At the present time, the increase of these productions is handicapped by a cost-price squeeze.
Our local production of feed grain covers only 60 to 65 per cent of our local requirements, at the present level of our livestock production. We could, of course, increase our local production of feed grain, but never enough to meet all our needs, especially in barley and wheat.
The subsidy rate did not keep pace with the increase in freight rates. In 1941, the subsidy represented in Montreal $4.50 per ton; today, it is equivalent to $5 per ton. During the same period, the freight rate increased from $5 to $13.20 per ton.
Most farmers and agricultural advisers in our cattle industry are aware of that fact.
When we get a department of agriculture for eastern Canada, it will be the reward for our efforts in Ottawa in order to gain a fair appreciation of our farm requirements.
We all have here a responsibility to change a state of affairs that means frustration for our rural population.
You are aware of the fact that people have been complaining to the government for a long time, and now is the time to act.
Finally, I should like to point out that the ARDA offices at Mont Joli, in the riding of Rimouski, were officially opened last December 8.
Federal and provincial ministers and members of parliament took advantage of the occasion to take a quick look at the projects which are being considered for the Rimouski-lower St. Lawrence pilot district.
ARDA forces neither plans nor projects upon people. It merely strives to help them in the preparation and implementation of plans and projects.
Its usefulness and efficiency in carrying out the various necessary reforms for the redevelopment of the territory covered by the pilot district will depend on the collective and individual co-operation of the parties concerned.
Our farmers truly deserve our solicitude and all men of goodwill are invited to contribute to their welfare and survival.
ARDA offers us a chance of progress and success. Will we take it? I hope so.

I just want to take a moment or two of the committee's time to mention one or two matters which occur to me. I
IMr. Ouellet.]
listened to some of the minister's remarks this evening and this afternoon. While he touched on several aspects of the dairy industry I feel that the affairs of the industry in general were not given the consideration they deserved.
The dairy industry in Ontario and Quebec at the present time finds itself in a precarious state. There are many problems connected with it. The minister and his department are familiar with these problems, I am sure, and I hope that in the near future, as soon as possible, the hon. gentleman will get in touch with the ministers of agriculture of Ontario and Quebec and with the dairy farmers organizations and try to work out some solution to the dairy problem, because the difficulties of this industry seem to be growing more and more acute.
In conclusion, I should like to ask one question of the minister. It is my understanding that the concentrated milk producers of Ontario have been trying for weeks to obtain an appointment with him without success. This is an important matter. This is an important organization representing a large number of the dairy farmers of Ontario and, indirectly, their compatriots in other parts of the country. I do hope the minister will be able to find time to meet this delegation as soon as possible.

I should like to answer that question. I can assure the hon. member my door is always open. There is no delegation that I have not seen as soon as possible. Over my gate back home there is a sign- I think it is a famous sign in Calgary now- saying: "The latch string is always out". That is the way I have tried to operate since I have been in Ottawa.
While I am on my feet, perhaps I might say a word about the discussion so far. I hope everybody has had a great deal of fun here this evening. Certainly, I have. If I have provided some of it, I am thankful for that. All through my life I have had a great admiration for people who do things and I would like hon. members to know that it is a great challenge to me to be Minister of Agriculture. I say this humbly. I do not have as much book learning as a lot of people have, but I have a sense of responsibility and I can contribute to agriculture. There has been a great group of leaders in agriculture before me; one cannot help being aware of this when holding an office such as mine. I am thankful that this year-perhaps we did not have too much to do with it-we are looking back on 1963 as the greatest agricultural year Canada has ever known-$3,200 million, the best ever recorded.
We are trying sincerely to do something about the eastern feed grain situation. We

thought that if we were to pay the storage it would make an impact. I think that by the end of the season we shall have all the feed grain in store in eastern Canada for eastern users. It will be $3 a ton cheaper for both oats and barley, half the price for bran, and shorts are almost half the price which farmers had to pay a year ago. Price has been stabilized and we think this has made some contribution to bringing about a wholly better situation.
We think we have done something in connection with the dairy program. We have taken a sincere look at it. In this connection I should like to read to the committee from an article which appeared in the London Free Press and other newspapers. It is a report of something which was said by a very responsible man, Mr. J. M. Hartwick, president of the National Dairy Council of Canada. He said:
A shift to cheese production from butter has helped provide the dairy industry with the most optimistic situation experienced in many years. It is now almost certain that Cheddar cheese sales in Canada this year will record an all-time high of well over 105 million pounds.
Mr. Hartwick commends the federal government for the things it has done. I could also read the favourable comments which have been made by the tobacco growers who were paid a floor price of 47 cents. These people had a difficult problem. Well, they have sold 22 million pounds of their tobacco at higher prices than have ruled for a long time, and it appears it will be possible for them to get rid of all their tobacco this year and clean up a problem which has worried them for a long time.
I could go on in this vein. There have been successes in nearly every field of agriculture although, maybe, we have not been selling this story hard enough. We still have a big job to do. We shall never be through. I have a great team behind me. These people are trying to help me and I need help, and I am getting some help from the other side, too. I think we can do a job for agriculture in Canada and I hope, in some small way, I can make a contribution.

I much appreciate the minister's answer. I hope he will indicate that he will see the Ontario concentrated milk producers delegation perhaps before Christmas, and, certainly, before the year is out. I am glad to see the minister is nodding in assent. That is fine. I trust the hon. gentleman was not referring to me when he suggested that some members might have been trying to have some fun at his expense, because that would certainly not be the case;
I regard this subject as being a very serious matter indeed.
Supply-Agriculture
I am glad the minister has said the things he did this evening indicating that he intends to take a serious look at the milk side of the dairy industry in particular, because that is the part of this industry which is in the most difficult position of all.
I do not intend to speak for very long on the estimates of this department.
Hear, hear.

I wonder if the supporters of the government are fearful I may get back at the Minister of Agriculture on the subject of eastern feed grain and the appointment of a minister of agriculture, east. I do not think they are too far wrong. I probably will not make the kind of speech that was made in Chicago. I have not got that kind of competence. I heard the minister say a few moments ago that he felt a little ill at ease after taking on such a ministry. We know he was a very successful man in his own line of business, but I must say that we cannot permit him to rely on experience of that kind so far as agriculture in Canada is concerned. In that regard I am referring particularly to the situation in the eastern part of Canada.
Eastern agriculture has been neglected and is in a pitiful state economically at the moment. I do not blame the Minister of Agriculture in office now. I blame those that were there before him and the governments that preceded the present government. I blame the Liberal government that was in power prior to the Conservative administration of 1958, and the Conservative administration which took power at that time. That Conversative government had 208 seats in the house and yet could not find any possible way to solve some of the problems of eastern Canadian agriculture.
I heard the minister say today that there are two broad groups of farmers, the qualified and the more or less marginal group. He forgot one group, those who are in such deep financial trouble at the moment, those who are in a hopeless situation at the moment in the eastern provinces, especially in the province of Quebec, who represent by far the majority of the farmers in these provinces.
We have farmers in Quebec who are leaving their farms today, and the same applies to New Brunswick. They are doing so for the simple reason they cannot make both ends meet. They are working in the same way they worked 20 years ago. They are still slaving from sunup to sundown. The only difference is that at the end of the year ends do not meet any more, financially. Even if we take just the two groups, the qualified and the marginal, those farmers

Supply-Agriculture
have financial troubles. Every single farmer has them. Some of them have more than others.
So far as the western farmers are concerned, the government looked into their troubles in 1935 and helped them to solve their financial troubles to a certain extent by stabilizing the price of their grain. In 1935 the government formed the Canadian wheat board, and I think every western farmer is very proud of the Canadian wheat board.
How proud the eastern farmers would be if they had an eastern feed grain board. They are waiting for the same type of governmental action that was taken in 1935 to solve the problems of the western farmers to be taken now to solve the problems of the eastern farmers. The eastern farmers are in a critical financial state. If we compare western farms and eastern farms we find that western Canada is a better grain producing region and the farms do not need the care and labour that has to be put into eastern farms. Western farmers have a capable organization to sell their wheat. The government has an eye on the matter and sees that it is done. The western farmers have a guaranteed price. They have a floor price on their wheat and they at least have that guarantee.
What has the eastern farmer got as a guarantee? First of all, he does not produce enough for his own needs. This year in the province of Quebec there is 45 per cent underproduction. Where is the organization on the part of the government? The eastern farmer has to go through co-operatives, mills, brokers, distributors right to the lakehead, every kind of organization imaginable, to get the feed grain necessary for the winter. At the moment he has a fairly difficult time obtaining it at a decent price or at a price that will permit him to continue farming. There is no stable price in eastern Canada.
I heard one member say today that a farmer can start to prepare livestock, and before the winter is over the price of feed grain has varied so much that it is utterly hopeless for him to make ends meet. In Geneva in 1959 there was an international conference to stabilize the price of wheat on the world market and to provide floor and ceiling prices. If that was good for the world, why can we not have a stabilized price in the province of Quebec and the eastern provinces generally? If you can stabilize the price of wheat going out of the country, why can you not stabilize the price of grain coming into the eastern provinces so that it will not be too expensive on the one hand, and so that it will not go too low in price on the other hand? At least the farmers would know within what limits the price would range.
[Mr. Langlois.l
How are we going to stabilize the price? How do we solve the problem in eastern Canada at the moment? We have discussed it for the past few weeks in the standing committee on agriculture. I heard one opposition member say that the government had a two price system in its election platform. Why not provide a two price system in eastern Canada and pay a subsidy on western feed grain and seed grain also, so that the farmers of eastern Canada could obtain grain at a reasonable price and could make both ends meet at the end of the year? At the same time this would assure that the western farmer would receive his price also. With a subsidy on grain coming into eastern Canada the eastern farmer could purchase grain at a price which would allow him to make both ends meet at the end of the year. His financial problems would be solved and those of the western farmer would also be solved.
Eastern farmers have nothing against western farmers. They know they are not getting too much for their wheat or feed grains. But eastern farmers also know one other fact. They know they are paying too much for feed grain in the eastern provinces, and I suggest that anybody who thinks this is not so should go and take over a farm in any constituency in eastern Canada. I can take the Minister of Agriculture, or the supposed eastern minister of agriculture, to my constituency and put them on a farm. Up until six or seven years ago there were many farms in the province of Quebec that had been free of debt since our ancestors came to this country. Why is it that the same men who up until that time had been able to operate these farms and to have money in the bank today are in debt to the farm loan board, are in great difficulty and are wondering how to make both ends meet in order to pay their debts? These men are moving off the farms at the age of 40 or 45 and going into the city to try to find work. Yet we wonder why we have unemployment. Do hon. members think those farmers do not want to work their farms? They certainly do. It is no more pleasant to starve in the city than to starve on their own farms, but they are being kicked off their farms because they cannot even pay the taxes.
There is a possible solution, if the government wants to listen to one-and I would ask some of the government members to listen. I hear some talking by Liberal members. They can talk if they like. They did their talking for the 22 years preceding 1958. Now, perhaps the farmer will wonder why he is in such a mess. Instead of telling the farmer to look at his administrative problems, the government might tell him to take a pencil and

calculate why he is in this position. If three-quarters of the farmers did this, they would not have lasted until now. They are always living in hope. When you make the calculation on paper, you destroy the castle of hope in which the farmer has lived, and you destroy any hope he has of pulling himself out of the financial situation in which he is today.
We need an eastern feed grain board for eastern Canada. This board should buy its grain direct from the Canadian wheat board, which sells grain for western farmers. If the law does not permit these direct sales, then the law should be amended. If this were done, we might have some control over the movement of wheat. At the moment we cannot follow the movement of wheat from western Canada to Port Arthur or Fort William and then through a zigzag line. We do not know where it goes. All we know is that the farmer is paying for it. We have agencies, and we do not want another agency added to the ones we already have. If you add another agency to the 20 we have, we will merely have 21 agencies. The twenty first agency will take a profit. What we want is one agency to negotiate with the Canadian wheat board so that we can buy wheat at the price at which the wheat board sells it.
Then, this agency should use the shortest and cheapest route to get the grain into the farmer's yard. The cheapest way for the farmer is the shortest way, and not this zigzag line the grain follows at the moment. If the grain is moved through an agency the government will have a certain amount of control and supervision over that agency. The minister wanted to have supervision of the grain by this agency. I can supervise somebody all I want, but if I have no power to stop him from going into a bank or a shop and robbing the place, I might as well not be there at all. We do not want a board to supervise; we want a board to act in distributing the grain and controlling the movement of the grain. Then, the representatives on that board could appear before the agriculture committee and we could question them.
Then, Mr. Chairman, the government could employ the eastern feed grain board to administer the subsidy which it gives to the eastern farmer, the subsidy on transportation. We do not know the amount of this subsidy. The government also gives a subsidy for storage and another subsidy for protecting the grain. If all these subsidies were given to the eastern feed grain board, then the price of grain to the farmer might be reduced. If the price were still too high, then the farmers could make representations to the government to the effect they needed greater subsidies to enable them to operate with a profit. We have farmers now who are willing to work,
Supply-Agriculture
but you will not keep them on the farms, you will not keep their sons on farms, as long as this situation exists.
The establishment of this eastern feed grain board would eliminate these excess profits taken by the agencies who handle the grain in its movement from the lakehead to the farmer. This board could also have some measure of control over the feed mill. How much do we pay for feed at the moment from the mill, what we call chop? I believe we pay anywhere from $5.90 to $6.50 per hundred pounds. Can the minister tell me he knows what is in that chop? If there is a nickel's worth of some ingredient added, can the minister say at the moment that is sufficient reason for raising the price 75 cents? Does he know the situation? Let him look into it and establish a decent price for feed from western Canada for the eastern farmer.
Let us consider the position of the hog raiser in eastern Canada at the moment. If he raises 100 hogs and calculates the cost of feed and his time, he will find he is going to come out $150 in the hole. This amounts to a loss of $1.50 per hog. At that rate, is the minister or anybody else going to stay on the farm? The farmers are the ones who are classified. They are always the ones on the receiving end. If a farmer sells a hog, it is going to be classified as a class A hog, and he will be paid for it. If it is a class B, he will be paid for that. If he sells a class C hog, he will get the price for class C. When the Minister of Agriculture walks into a butcher shop, he buys a piece of pork. Did he ever buy a piece of class A, class B or class C? He might be buying a class C piece of pork but paying the price for class A. There are no distinguishing marks on that pork. However, everything the farmer sells is classified. The department classifies chickens, eggs and hogs. The farmer is a classified man, even in so far as the income tax department is concerned. He is also a desperate man, and he will be ruined if the minister does not take his responsibility seriously.
The minister can refer all he likes to the minister of agriculture for eastern Canada. If the government gave the eastern minister of agriculture responsibility for this feed grain board, and if it were operated properly, that would suffice for the eastern farmer. This would permit the eastern farmer to make both ends meet. Perhaps it would enable the eastern farmer to get a little more for his produce, and this would give him something above his cost of production. There are only two solutions to this problem, and I think the one I mentioned first would be the logical one. If a government agency for wheat sales was good for western Canada, it should be good for eastern Canada. If a stabilized price for wheat

Supply-Agriculture
is good for the international wheat market, it should be good for eastern Canada as well. We should do these things at home before we put them on a worldwide basis. I do not blame this government for helping the western farmer; he needed it. Our greatest market for wheat is the export market. I believe, for that reason, we have forgotten about our internal market. It is high time we started thinking about it.
The eastern farmer sees ships containing millions of bushels of wheat going up the St. Lawrence destined for China, Yugoslavia and Russia. It is all very nice that we are selling our wheat, but the eastern farmers are grinding their teeth. Eastern farmers are looking at these ships with anxiety and with sorrowful hearts, knowing that we are selling wheat to Poland cheaper than they can buy their feed wheat. Farmers are wondering why the government is worrying about Russia and Yugoslavia, because they think it is time the government started worrying about the Canadian people on Canadian farms. Then, when Canadian farmers are satisfied, you can start selling wheat outside of Canada. This is the primary problem to be solved at the moment.
I do not understand a situation which prevents the eastern farmer from buying wheat directly from the wheat board. But you can do it with United States corn. In 1962-63, 35 million bushels of United States corn came into eastern Canada. There is one group of persons that can buy from western farmers directly; these are the feed mills and the western flour mills. Nobody else has such a privilege. In fact, when you buy corn from the United States you do not even need a permit; you only need to pay the duty on it. You can take all the corn you want. But you cannot do it with Canadian wheat. Before putting boundaries in your own country you should solve this problem. You are creating problems when you put a boundary between eastern and western Canada with regard to grain.
It is no better to put a boundary between eastern and western Canada with regard to grain than if you put one between the United States and this country and started imposing taxes and duties on every single import or export that went through. We have special exports and imports that are duty free. This is a normal thing and it is a good thing. This system is adopted by both countries. We need grain in both countries. Either take the wall away or set up an organization that can go through the wall. This would be an eastern feed board. Nobody else can go through this wall because of the law. Not only would there be supervision with such a board, but somebody would be responsible for control.

In the long run this would bring good results. You will have to perhaps eliminate some things. It will be hard to push aside some of the people who have their hands in this business at the moment. There are some people at the moment who have no conscience in their dealings. You have some racketeers in this business. You have always had some. You had some in 1935 in western Canada. You still have some in eastern Canada. You will have trouble pushing them aside, but as long as you permit some of these rats that are eating at and chewing away the rules that apply to Canadian agriculture you will not solve this problem. Do not try to cover it by a Liberal or Conservative blanket. At the end of three or four years these rats will have eaten the blanket too and we will have to change the government. This government should try to arrive at a solution that on a long term basis would be stable and good for western and eastern farmers. Then you might have a higher prestige as the government of Canada; but at the moment your prestige is very low as far as the farmers in the eastern provinces are concerned.
If the problem is not solved before you next go to the Canadian people, you will have a great deal of explaining to do. And if it is not solved I will also be there to give the people the reason for your not wanting to solve the problem.

Mr. Chairman, I am very happy to have the opportunity this evening to speak on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I have waited since May 18 for just this opportunity. There have not been too many times when we have been able to speak about agriculture, and when we have said something we have not got very far with it. I am very sorry that the hour is so late. It is ten minutes after ten o'clock and I believe our sitting will finish at 10.30.
Ten fifteen.

Therefore, Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief, much more brief than I intended. Before beginning my remarks I want to say how impressed I am with the address of the hon. member for Megantic who preceded me. I think he has put forward as good a case for the farmers of Quebec as I have ever heard. For the life of me I cannot understand why, in the name of God, something has not been done for the farmers of eastern Canada to help them out over the years. We in the west were in exactly the same position up till 1957. Last year we heard a great deal about the fact that if a farmer in Quebec made $1,200 a year profit he felt almost like a millionaire. That is the way it was in the west with most of us up

till 1957. There were many things I wanted to say to the minister, Mr. Chairman, but I will not say them because of the lateness of the hour.
There are, however, a few things I do want to point out. I want the minister to know that I realize how difficult it must be for him to live up to the tenets of a district governor of the Rotary club and be at the same time a minister in a Liberal government. This must be really tough on him. As we know, the first of the tenets of the Rotary club is truth. He cannot always have Judy with him. I wanted to make some remarks about the speech of the hon. member for Medicine Hat, but I think the hon. member for Acadia gave him a pretty good going over. I will come back to that hon. member a little later.
I wish to say one thing about the farmers of eastern Canada who buy feed grain. Perhaps people in the east do not know that the farmers of western Canada pay the freight on the grain, whether it is feed grain or wheat, all the way to the lakehead or Vancouver. It costs every farmer who sells grain 26 cents per 100 pounds to ship the grain down there. We have only that small amount to pay because of the Crowsnest pass freight rate, the agreement which gives us that freight rate to the lakehead. This rate is in effect because of agreements made in the past and because the transcontinental railway companies were well paid when they ran their railways through our country. They obtained one eighteenth of the land of western Canada in payment for continuing these low freight rates in perpetuity.
I should like to make some comments about the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and crop insurance. The government of the province of Alberta has not yet seen fit to do anything about implementing crop insurance in our province. I know they are talking about it this year, and they may do it some time. I think this government should make amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which will make its benefits available to all farmers. This would be fair to all. At the moment, in order to receive prairie farm assistance you must have a block of 12 sections in a rectangular block which has suffered a crop failure. I think this is too much. Who in the world ever heard of rain, hail, drought, or any other cause of failure, coming in rectangular blocks? I do not know why in all these years since 1939 a farmer is not eligible to receive assistance if he has a block of one section, because I can assure the committee that misfortune does not always hit 12 sections or, as it was before, 18 sections.
In 1962 in my constituency about 30 townships were flooded out. They had as much 28902-5-369
Supply-Agriculture
as 35 inches of rainfall in an area where 12 inches or 15 inches a year is a lot. The farmers lost their whole crop on the lowlands, but they did not get prairie farm assistance because some of them sowed a little on the hilltops and were able to harvest pretty good crops off the 10 or 15 acres that they sowed there. For the purposes of assistance the whole area was assessed on the amount taken off those little patches, and I believe that is a regulation which should be changed.
I would like to see this government honour its commitments to provide stabilized prices for hogs and chickens on a regional basis. I know this will be quite difficult to do, and I would also like to see the government fulfil its promise to provide a two price system for wheat. Most of all, I would like to see the Prairie Farm Assistance Act brought up to date and its provisions made more reasonable, so that all those farmers who have not been able to get assistance over the years will be able to get it in the future.
With regard to machinery prices, I do not know what kind of deal the minister hopes to work out on a rental basis for farm machinery. As a matter of fact, I would like to rent a nice big tractor myself at a reasonable price, as mine are getting a little worn out. It is the price of farm machinery which keeps the farmers in the west almost broke. For example, 20 years ago the biggest combine in the country could be bought for the value of between 2,500 and 3,000 bushels of wheat. It now costs something between the value of 9,000 and 10,000 bushels of wheat. It is a little better machine, a little more streamlined, but it will not stand up a darned bit better. It will do a little more work a little bit faster, but the increase in price is out of all reason because the price of farm produce has not gone up in ratio to the price of machinery.
I was a member of the agriculture committee when it was inquiring into the price of farm machinery. We did not get too far with it, but we did get a lot of information that might be of assistance to the minister who wants to have the government go into the farm machinery business. All I can say is that I wish him luck.
We in the west are very pleased that the government is continuing the practice that was instituted by its immediate predecessor in selling grain to countries who do not have the same political ideology we have. I have always said that if we do not sell grain to those people-despite what our friends to my left say-and that if we do not deal with them, then how in the name of God are we going to get to know each other? How are we

Supply-Agriculture
going to get people to realize that there are really decent people behind the iron curtain? That is what I believe and that is what I have always preached.
It they need the grain, sell it to them. We sure as heck don't need it piled up on farms, in skating rinks, or anywhere tor that matter. The big thing is that we are a producing nation, and in order to survive we have got to sell our products. That is what has to be accomplished, and that is what was instituted by the former government through its minister of agriculture, the Hon. Alvin Hamilton. It was that which put the farmers of western Canada on their feet.
The former Liberal government said "Come and get it. We raise the best wheat in the world, come and get it." We went to these people and we made the deals. We did not wait to deal with them until they came to Ottawa and said they wanted to make a deal. However, we are very pleased that this government is continuing that policy.
We are also pleased to note that a veterinary college is to be established in western Canada. For many years there has been a dearth of veterinarians, and it will be a very good thing to have this college.
I now wish to make some remarks about farm credit. I believe that my constituency, while it is one of the most prosperous and most forward looking constituencies in the west, makes more use of farm credit than any other area of similar size in the country.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. I should like to suggest a slight modification in the order of arrangements for tomorrow, but, before I do that, hon. members will have noticed that the somewhat belated resolution respecting the worlds fair bill was advanced one stage today. We would not wish to have any debate on it, but if there were a disposition to dispose of it without debate so that the bill might become available for debate on Monday, it would be a convenience. Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite could let me know before we sit tomorrow morning whether that would be possible.
As far as the departments are concerned, the Minister of Justice finds he has committed himself to do something in the afternoon, tomorrow, and it would suit the government much better if we could begin with the estimates of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. If we could take the Department of Fisheries and any

other department whose estimates are already well advanced, up until about four thirty in the afternoon, I believe the Minister of Justice would then be available, and we could then go on with his estimates until they were completed. We would always have some other minister available in the event that anything more could be done that day.
On Saturday, as I announced earlier, we would start with the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. When these are completed, if the estimates of the
Business of the House
Department of Justice have not been completed we would like to bring those back in the hope of completing them. After that we would take up the estimates of the Department of Public Works. That, perhaps, would be enough for Saturday. If the estimates of the Department of Public Works were completed on Saturday we would adjourn even if it was not quite six o'clock.

It being twenty two minutes before eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
